The DEATH BETS Act is the first bill regulating prediction markets to pass in the Senate in the 119 th Congress Washington, D.C. — Today, the U.S. Senate unanimously passed U.S. Senator Adam Schiff’s (D-Calif.) and John Curtis’ (R-Utah), DEATH BETS Act , legislation to explicitly prohibit any Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC)-registered entity from listing any contract that references terrorism, assassination, war, United States Armed Forces military operations, or an individual’s death. Schiff, a member of the Senate Agriculture Committee, first introduced this bill in March 2026. Representative Mike Levin (D-Calif-49) introduced companion legislation in the U.S. House of Representatives. Senator Schiff delivered remarks on the Senate floor moments before the bill passed and was joined by Senator Curtis. Watch his full speech HERE. “Betting on war and death jeopardizes our national security by creating a perverse environment in which violence is incentivized and insiders are allowed to profit off privileged or classified information. There is no justification for gambling on lives, or public benefit to be derived by such a market. With my bill, Congress is making it clear today that these death bets should be unlawful,” said Senator Schiff. “No one should be able to wager on terrorism, war, or the death of another human being,” said Senator Curtis . “There is a fundamental difference between legitimate financial markets and gambling on human suffering. The DEATH BETS Act draws a clear moral line by prohibiting these types of wagers on federally regulated exchanges.” Under the Commodity Exchange Act , the CFTC currently has the authority to prohibit war, terrorism, and assassination contracts from being listed if they are determined by the Commission to be contrary to the public interest. Whether or not these contracts are in the public interest is at the discretion of the CFTC. At a time when CFTC Chair Selig has indicated that he will rewrite the rules on prediction markets, the CFTC can no longer be granted this discretion. This bill will unequivocally ban these contracts. According to public reporting, there have been numerous cases this year in which individuals were suspected to have traded on prediction markets to profit from inside information related to war and U.S. Armed Services actions. Lawmakers have previously raised the alarm to the CFTC on these “death contracts” being offered on offshore exchanges, such as on whether or not Artemis II would explode, Maduro would be removed from power, or the Ukrainian town of Myrnohad would be captured by Russian forces. The DEATH BETS Act specifically would: Codify a prohibition on war, assassination, and terrorism contracts. Explicitly prohibit contracts that involve an individual’s death, which is not currently referenced in the Commodity Exchange Act . The full text of the bill is available here. Read the full transcript of his remarks as delivered below: Senator Adam Schiff: Mr. President, I’m here today to urge the Senate to pass legislation that I’m proud to lead along with Senator John Curtis, the DEATH BETS Act . Over the last two years, the rapid growth prediction markets has allowed users to gamble on just about anything. Just this year, we’ve seen these markets offer wagers on whether the Artemis II mission and its four astronauts would explode. It created a market on whether Nicolas Maduro would be removed from power in Venezuela. It even offered a potential profit for those who could correctly predict whether a Ukrainian town of Myrnohrad would be captured by Russia. In many cases, these contracts offered were offered in contravention of state and Tribal law. They create rampant opportunities for insider trading, and perhaps worst of all, they are offered with no regard for national security and, in far too many cases, even basic morality. These markets are operating in a wild west, desperately in need of regulation and guardrails. Today, we have the opportunity to put into place a very simple rule: the first building block to create one of those guardrails. Our bill prohibits prediction markets from offering contracts on war, military operations, and death, Betting and profiting off of death, both in tragedy and in war, is immoral and ought to be unlawful. Indeed, many of us believe it already is. But the regulators at CFTC, or in this case, regulator, is not only hands off. He’s acting as the legal infantry for the industry, attempting to preempt state laws and challenging them whenever his agency is unsuccessful. As a result, the CFTC has created a system with the most perverse incentives that would reward betting on a mass casualty event. A market that one could easily imagine would actually encourage lethal events and jeopardize our national security for the right amount of money. It’s a whole new version of the very idea of a contract kill. Take the real-life example we’ve seen on these platforms: people placing bets on wildfires, wagering on how devastating they could be; people placing bets on every twist and turn in the war with Iran, sometimes with inside information, motivated by the same underlying principle of financial markets and gaming conventions, the possibility of profit. But these are not regulated financial markets; they’re not seen by the administration as sports betting or gambling, even though such illegal practices are widespread and the subject of yet another bill that Senator Curtis and I are leading. There’s no justification for gambling on lives or public benefit to be derived by such a market. It’s dangerous and it’s wrong. In the absence of real leadership and enforcement at the CFTC, it’s time for Congress to step in and fix this problem. With our bill, Congress is making clear that these bets should be illegal once and for all. Simply put, the legislation we are enacting today is a targeted fix of a single pressing problem. The sole purpose of the DEATH BETS Act is to make clear that betting on war, death, military operations, and similar circumstances is unlawful. But we also want to make clear that the legislation has no effect whatsoever on pending litigation regarding whether sports contracts offered by prediction markets qualify as swaps or other derivatives under federal law, or on whether federal derivatives laws preempt state gaming and consumer protection laws regarding such sports contracts. We’ve included a rule of construction in the DEATH BETS Act designed to make this crystal clear. Per that rule, no part of this bill will affect the permissibility of any sports contracts or similar agreements. If sports contracts are impermissible under federal or state law today, as I, and many others believe they are, it will remain impermissible after this legislation is enacted. We are aware that there is active litigation across the country on swaps and preemption issues. Nothing in the DEATH BETS Act should have any effect on those lawsuits, and it would be improper to draw any inference from this bill that other federal statutes or regulations should be interpreted in a particular way, or that Congress has expressed any intent on how the issues in litigation should be decided. Nor should the DEATH BETS Act be construed as providing the CFTC with authority to authorize or regulate sports contracts on prediction markets. The CFTC has no expertise with respect to gaming. The states and Tribes have long served as the nation’s gaming regulators, and nothing Congress is doing today displaces that traditional state and Tribal authority. Indeed, the CFTC’s recent actions to attempt to assist prediction markets in litigation confirm that the CFTC has strayed far outside its authority. Sports contracts are sports bets in disguise. The CFTC’s job is to promote fair competition and market efficiency, not to serve as a nationwide sports betting regulator. This bill is a commonsense step, and merely the first to rein in a runaway prediction market regulation that violates state law and Tribal sovereignty, common sense, and our values. I want to again thank my colleague Senator Curtis for his advocacy and leadership, not just on this bill but on a broader issue, and I would be proud to yield to Senator Curtis. ###

Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) introduced The Women Economic Fairness and Small Business Contracting Act , legislation to increase opportunities for women-owned small businesses by tripling the federal contracting goal and offering different pathways for women entrepreneurs to grow their business. “Small businesses are vital to our communities and economy, and women-owned small businesses, in particular, make up over 40% of all U.S. businesses. They would grow even faster if they had good and fair opportunities to compete for federal contracts. My legislation will open more doors for women entrepreneurs and level the playing field,” said Senator Schiff. The Women Economic Fairness and Small Business Contracting Act will: Increase the Women Owned Small Business (WOSB) Federal Prime subcontracting goal from 5 percent to 15 percent; Raise the government-wide small business contracting set-aside goal from 23 percent to 33 percent; and Require the Small Business Administrations (SBA) to meet or exceed its annual prime contracting goals. U.S. Senator Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.) is a cosponsor. The bill is endorsed by the American Small Business League. “Working with Senator Schiff to raise the federal contracting goal for women-owned small businesses from 5% to 15% is an important step toward opening doors to the nation’s largest marketplace and giving women entrepreneurs the opportunities they deserve,” said Lloyd Chapman, President of the American Small Business League. “I applaud Senator Schiff for standing up for women-owned businesses and for America’s small businesses. Every small business owner in this country should know that Senator Schiff is fighting for them and working to ensure they have a meaningful opportunity to compete, grow and succeed.” The full text of the legislation is available here . ###

Washington, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senators Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla (both D-Calif.) announced that their bicameral and bipartisan bills to promote Tribal management of over 800 acres of land in California passed in the Senate and House of Representatives. The Pit River Land Transfer Act and Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians Land Transfer Act now head to President Trump’s desk to be signed into law. “For generations, California’s tribes have fought to rightfully restore their ancestral homelands and preserve the culture of their ancestors,” said Senator Schiff . “I am proud Congress has passed our legislation to help the Pit River Tribe and Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians reclaim their cultural lands and promote tribal sovereignty.” “For too long, California’s Tribal nations have been denied the right to manage and preserve their ancestral lands. The historic passage of these two bills represents a key step toward righting our historical wrongs,” said Senator Padilla. “Restoring tribal land to its original owners preserves traditions, strengthens communities, and supports ecological health across California. I am proud to support the Pit River Tribe and the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians and I am grateful for the bipartisan, bicameral support that made these land transfers possible.” Pit River Land Transfer Act This bill would transfer 557 acres of federal land administered by the United States Forest Service to the Department of the Interior to be held in trust for the Pit River Tribe. The Tribe has been actively trying to acquire this land through various governmental processes for over a decade. However, they have experienced a series of delays that have added years to the process. The late Representative Doug LaMalfa (R-Calif.-01) led companion legislation in the House of Representatives, which is now led by Representative James Gallagher (R-Calif.-01). “Doug LaMalfa was a tireless advocate for the North State, and returning this land to the Pit River Tribe was a cause he believed in,” said Representative Gallagher . “I’m honored to carry his work forward and grateful to Senator Padilla for his partnership in moving this legislation through the Senate. The Tribe has waited more than a decade for this, and it’s encouraging to see Republicans and Democrats working together to get it across the finish line.” “For the Pit River Tribe, Four Corners is more than a parcel of land. It is a place that connects our ancestors, our history, and our future,” said Pit River Tribe Chairman Yatch Bamford . “Passage of this legislation brings us closer to caring for this land as its Stewards, preserving a site central to our people’s struggle for justice, and creating a place where future generations can learn our history. We thank Senator Padilla for his leadership and tireless work in securing passage of this bill, and Senator Schiff for his support. We are also deeply grateful to the late Congressman Doug LaMalfa for his leadership and work to advance this legislation. Their commitments to our Tribe made this milestone possible, as we work toward a future rooted in our culture and shaped by our people.” The Pit River Tribe consist of 11 autonomous bands traditionally inhabiting the area surrounding the Pit River and its tributaries. They are known for their deep spiritual connection to the land, with a rich cultural heritage centered around fishing, hunting, and seasonal gatherings. The proposed land to be transferred is known as the Four Corners Property, located in Shasta County. The Tribe has strong cultural and historical connections to the Four Corners, and they view it as a central landmark of their ancestral lands. In October 1970, members of the Tribe erected a Quonset hut on the Four Corners, staking a peaceful, yet firm claim. That month, over 100 sheriff’s deputies, federal marshals, and forest rangers ordered the occupants to evacuate the property, which eventually resulted in violence and the hospitalization of several Tribal members. Full text of the Pit River Land Transfer Act is available here . Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians Land Transfer Act This bill would place approximately 80 acres of land currently managed by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) into trust for the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians, a federally recognized Tribe whose reservation is located near Placerville in the western Sierra Nevada foothills. The bill would also place into trust 185 acres of fee land already owned by the Tribe. Representative Tom McClintock (R-Calif.-05) is leading companion legislation in the House of Representatives. “The Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians survived near annihilation during the Spanish and Gold Rush eras to become a prosperous and integral part of El Dorado County. I am honored to carry this legislation that will continue their progress and contributions to their posterity and to our community into the years ahead,” said Representative McClintock . “This legislation is about our homeland and the future we are building for our children and grandchildren,” said Chairwoman Regina Cuellar . “Its passage brings us closer to securing these lands for our people and strengthening our ability to care for them for generations to come. We thank Senators Padilla and Schiff and Congressman McClintock for their leadership and work to secure passage of this legislation. We are deeply grateful for their commitment to our Tribe and support for our future.” The Tribe’s current trust land base is just 317 acres and their reservation access was significantly disrupted decades ago when Highway 50 was constructed across their only entrance. While the Tribe has since invested in an off-ramp to restore access, their existing land remains insufficient to meet the needs of their citizens. This bill would place BLM land into trust for the Tribe to maintain it for open space and fire risk management. By enabling the Tribe to place their existing fee land into trust, the bill would help the Tribe build much-needed housing. Full text of the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians Land Transfer Act is available here . ###

Washington, D.C. – During a Senate Agriculture Committee hearing today considering nominations to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) called out CFTC Chairman Michael Selig for misleading the Committee while under oath on his stance on prediction markets. Schiff highlighted that despite Selig previously telling the Committee that he would “follow what the courts say,” under his unilateral leadership, the CFTC has intervened in prediction market litigation and sued 12 states for attempting to enforce their own gambling laws. “Over the last two years, the rapid growth of prediction markets has allowed users to gamble on just about anything…These markets are operating in a Wild West, desperately in need of regulation and guardrails,” Senator Schiff said during the exchange. “ During his confirmation hearing, I asked Chairman Selig a simple question of whether a prediction contract on who wins or loses a football game is sports betting. He told me that he would be a blank slate on whether prediction markets were gambling and that he would defer to the courts… But he has been anything but a blank slate. He has not looked to the courts. He’s filed briefs to tell the courts what to do, and when the courts have ruled in a way that doesn’t favor the prediction markets, he has basically told companies to ignore the courts, ignore court orders, don’t geofence, don’t respect state or Tribal laws. Anything but a blank slate. I don’t know that I’ve ever been so blatantly deceived by a nominee before” Senator Schiff said. Schiff also pressed Nathan Amonick, nominee to be Commissioner of the CFTC, on whether he would defer to the courts and respect state and Tribal laws on prediction market regulation. Since his confirmation, Chairman Selig has yet to appear before the Senate Agriculture Committee. Watch the full clip here Read the full transcript below: Schiff: Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Mr. Anonick, and Mr. Rowland, congratulations on your nominations. Thank you for your service to the Committee and to the Senate. Currently, we have only one Senate-confirmed Commissioner, and I’m glad that the Committee is considering a bipartisan pair of Commissioner nominees today, it is long overdue. Over the last two years, the rapid growth of prediction markets has allowed users to gamble on just about anything. In many cases, these contracts are offered in direct contravention of state and tribal law. They create rampant opportunities for insider trading. Too often, they are offered with no regard for national security or even basic morality. The rapid growth of these prediction markets has been fueled by billions of dollars in sports betting, illegally offered on prediction market platforms in all 50 states and on tribal lands. These markets are operating in a wild west, desperately in need of regulation and guardrails. During his confirmation hearing, I asked Chairman Selig a simple question of whether a prediction contract on who wins or loses a football game is sports betting. He told me that he would be a blank slate on whether prediction markets were gambling and that he would defer to the courts. In fact, I can’t tell you how many times he told me exactly that, “Mr. Senator,” he said. “It would be irresponsible for me to prejudge that issue. I will look to the courts.” In answer to another question, “Senator, I, again, would look to the courts on these questions of facts and interpretation of the law. It’s a complex issue. I will follow what the courts say.” And again, “Senator, on this issue, I would look to the courts. So, I would look to what the courts say about the issue.” And I asked him if I’m betting on a Bills game, or what would you say about that? “Well, there are many lengthy opinions have been written on one word in statute, and I want the benefit of understanding what the judges think about the issue,” and again, “I think it would be irresponsible for me to prejudge that issue.” And so, I would come to the issue, into the issue at the commission, have confirmed with a blank slate, and look to the courts, because I asked him whether he had a preconceived idea, whether he was a tabula rasa, he said he was a blank slate. Well, I don’t know whether he was just lying to us, or once he was confirmed, he had some kind of an epiphany. But he has been anything but a blank slate. He has not looked to the courts. He’s filed briefs to tell the courts what to do, and when the courts have ruled in a way that doesn’t favor the prediction markets, he has basically told companies to ignore the courts, ignore court orders, don’t geofence, don’t respect state or tribal laws. Anything but a blank slate. I don’t know that I’ve ever been so blatantly deceived by a nominee before. This is certainly not the kind of leadership that we need at CFTC. So, Mr. Anonick, let me ask you really the same question I asked him: If I bet using a prediction market on who will win this Thursday’s NFL game between the Colts and the Texans, is that a sports bet? Nathan Anonick: Senator, thank you for that question, and I can only speak for myself, not anyone else. I do think that question, from a legal perspective, is complex, and that federal courts have disagreed on that. Schiff: Okay, but is it really complex? I mean, if we’re betting on who wins a football game on Thursday night, it kind of sounds like a sports bet, right? Anonick: I certainly appreciate the practical argument. I just say it’s legally complex. Schiff: If betting on who wins a football game is not a sports bet, can you tell me what a sports bet is? Anonick: I agree, Senator, that the fact that there’s been different federal courts’ opinions makes that question confusing. But it is an issue that the federal courts have disagreed with. Again, I can only speak for myself, Senator. Schiff : Well, let me ask you: Are you a tabula rasa? Are you a blank slate? Are you going to defer to the courts, or are you going to act like our current Chairman and tell the courts what to do? Anonick : Senator, if confirmed, the Supreme Court reaches a decision on this. I would fully support that the CFTC needs to follow that decision, regardless of the decision. Schiff : And are you going to take a position in that litigation and tell the Supreme Court that you think that states and Tribes should not have a say; that companies should ignore court orders if they don’t defer to the CFTC and its jurisdiction. Is that the position you’re going to take, the same as the Chair? Anonick : Senator, I’m not trying to be evasive. I don’t know a position I would take on anything. If I was confirmed and there was a matter before me, and I would take the role as Commissioner seriously. I think that means a robust, thorough fact-finding process. That means talking to Office of General Counsel. That means talking to outside counsel, that means talking to the Tribes and the states and all of the stakeholders. And anything before me would be my own decision, and I would own that. But out of respect for the seriousness that I think being a commissioner requires, and going through that robust process, I don’t have a preconceived position because it would be irresponsible of me to make that position until I’ve gone through that process. Schiff: I just hope that I don’t have another confirmation hearing for another proposed nominee and have to read your testimony back. I hope you’ll be true to what you’ve just said, and approach this with an open mind, and hear the stakeholders, including the states and the Tribes, and their perspective before you make a judgment. I thank you, Mr. Chairman. I yield back. ###

Washington, D.C. — U.S. Senators Adam Schiff, Alex Padilla (both D-Calif.), Ron Wyden, Jeff Merkley (both D-Ore.), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), and Ed Markey (D-Mass.) launched an inquiry into the Trump Administration’s politically motivated campaign against state Medicaid programs, after the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) withheld billions of dollars from Democratic-led states while dismantling the federal infrastructure designed to detect and prevent fraud. In their letter to CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, the Senators explained that CMS attacks on state Medicaid programs have undermined fraud-prevention infrastructure within the federal government and targeted Democratic-led states. “The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services is running the most aggressive public enforcement campaign against state Medicaid programs in the agency’s history, while accelerating the systematic dismantling of the federal infrastructure Congress funded to prevent Medicaid fraud in the first place,” the lawmakers wrote . “That is not program integrity. That is political theater layered over a decade of neglect, with states across the country, and in particular, an overwhelming number of Democratic-led states that have become the Trump administration’s targets, left to answer for both.” The letter comes as the Trump Administration has threatened state health programs with severe funding cuts based on flawed data. CMS recently moved to withhold billions in funding from California and Minnesota without providing any evidence of wrongdoing to the states. At the same time, the Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS OIG) decertified state Medicaid Fraud Control Units (MFCUs) in Hawaii and New York. Public reporting, including an investigation by the Associated Press , revealed that the Administration’s fraud claims against New York relied on a basic math error, while other withholding actions have sparked lawsuits from states like Minnesota. Rather than working with states to fix issues, CMS has replaced on-site reviews and dedicated oversight staff with a public relations “War Room” and artificial intelligence pilots. The letter points out that the Administration is violating federal law by failing to maintain the minimum required funding and staffing levels for the Medicaid Integrity Program, which was created by Congress to help states fight fraud. Full text of the letter is available here and below: Administrator Oz: The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) is running the most aggressive public enforcement campaign against state Medicaid programs in the agency’s history, while accelerating the systematic dismantling of the federal infrastructure Congress funded to prevent Medicaid fraud in the first place. That is not program integrity. That is political theater layered over a decade of neglect, with states across the country, and in particular, an overwhelming number of Democratic-led states that have become the Trump administration’s targets, left to answer for both. Since you were confirmed as Administrator, you sent all 50 governors letters demanding provider revalidation on a ten-business-day clock. You moved to withhold more than $2 billion annually in federal Medicaid funds from Minnesota without providing the State any details on its alleged noncompliance, and then issued successive deferral actions in February, April, and July 2026 totaling more than $500 million in additional federal Medicaid funds. In successive deferral actions in May, July, and October 2026, you also withheld more than $3.4 billion in federal Medicaid funds tied to California’s In-Home Supportive Services program and personal care services, citing nothing more than California’s growth rate relative to other states, with no specific evidence of wrongdoing. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS OIG) has decertified Hawaii and New York’s Medicaid Fraud Control Units and placed all 53 Medicaid Fraud Control Units (MFCUs) under review. Though most MFCUs are housed within state Attorneys General offices, all serve as the primary mechanism for prosecuting Medicaid provider fraud; consequently, decertifying them in the name of fighting fraud is self-defeating. Moreover, while statutory oversight of MFCUs rests with HHS OIG, the CMS Center for Program Integrity (CPI), whose statutory role is to serve as the federal bridge to state MFCUs so that state Medicaid program integrity units work in partnership with and refer cases to their respective MFCUs, has provided no visible support to states navigating this review. During New York’s decertification, it appears that CPI provided no technical assistance or support to the program integrity unit, leaving state investigators without a functioning federal pathway. Instead, you have launched a Medicaid Fraud “War Room” that your Deputy Administrator publicly calls “what modern program integrity looks like.” Modern program integrity should start with meeting the mandates Congress already wrote into law. Medicaid program integrity has been under-resourced across administrations. That is precisely why Congress established the Medicaid Integrity Program (MIP) in the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005 and imposed a statutory floor of no less than $75 million and no fewer than 100 full-time employees (FTEs) dedicated annually to working collaboratively with states to fight Medicaid provider fraud and abuse. At the same time, Congress enacted mandatory federal technical assistance, on-site state reviews, and analytical support to states. Those obligations are not discretionary, and CMS cannot treat dedicated funding as optional funding or repurpose it at will. The Trump administration and CMS under your leadership are not meeting these binding statutory obligations. Instead, you are hollowing out MIP under the guise of enforcement and compounding institutional failures: The Division of Fraud Research and Detection, the only CMS division dedicated exclusively to Medicaid analytics, which maintained direct data feeds from approximately sixteen states’ Medicaid Management Information Systems (MMIS), was eliminated in the 2015 CPI reorganization. The defining failure of the current era is that these vital tools were never rebuilt, allowing what was once a temporary reorganization to harden into a permanent blind spot. Comprehensive on-site State Program Integrity Reviews have been replaced with remote “Focused Reviews” issuing non-binding “Observations.” CMS no longer tells states what to fix; it tells states what to consider. Until this administration, even as the MIP infrastructure weakened, CMS and states maintained a working collaborative relationship on program integrity – sharing data, issuing joint fraud alerts with HHS OIG, and working through disallowances backed by evidence. That collaborative posture has been replaced by performative enforcement. The Medicaid Integrity Institute’s residential training at the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) Ernest F. Hollings National Advocacy Center (NAC), CMS’s flagship in-person training for state program integrity staff, has been eliminated in favor of an all-virtual calendar. State program integrity directors have asked, in every available forum, for the in-person peer-led instruction to return, and CMS has refused. Public reporting and CMS’s own training calendars indicate the Institute has been reduced to a handful of virtual webinars per year and a few regional in-person listening sessions with State Medicaid Agencies and MFCUs between July and November 2026. Publicly reported accounts indicate the federal workforce dedicated exclusively to Medicaid program integrity has fallen dramatically below the 100-FTE floor Congress set. CMS state liaisons, fraud alerts issued jointly with HHS OIG, State Medicaid Director letters on program integrity, and the Annual Summary Report of Program Integrity Reviews have all been eliminated or discontinued. An enforcement campaign built on gutted infrastructure produces shoddy results. On April 10, 2026, news reports revealed that CMS acknowledged its fraud probe of New York Medicaid rested on a figure that was off by a factor of ten – a basic mathematical error in calculating annual unique beneficiaries that independent analysts traced to a fundamental misunderstanding of how Medicaid data is counted. The administration publicly shared whatever figures served its political purposes, and the resulting mistake was then used to threaten a state. California has faced a separate but equally troubling pattern: CMS has imposed federal payment deferrals that have now accumulated to more than $3.4 billion, with California’s Medicaid director publicly rejecting the validity of CMS’s claims and stating that CMS has provided no evidence supporting the deferrals. Minnesota has gone further and filed suit against CMS, HHS, you, and Secretary Kennedy over the attempted withholding of $243 million in Medicaid payments, alleging that CMS imposed the withholding, without informing the state, despite it asking repeatedly, how it was noncompliant or what corrective steps were required. CMS is putting on theatrics about going after states to “crush fraud” without any legitimate data to back up their claims, all the while starving the federal office Congress created to help states prevent those failures. A fake war room is not a substitute for a Medicaid integrity program that meets its statutory obligations. Contracting Medicaid analytics out to General Dynamics Information Technology (GDIT), the current Trusted Third Party for the Healthcare Fraud Prevention Partnership (HFPP), a multi-payer public-private partnership, is also not in compliance with a statute that requires Medicaid-dedicated federal capacity. On October 15, 2026, your Deputy Administrator announced at an industry conference that CMS is piloting artificial intelligence to flag suspicious Medicaid billing patterns “in near real-time before Medicaid payments are made,” with the stated goal of scaling the pilots into a “national, standardized, continuously improving platform.” CMS does not, however, operate the claims systems that generate the underlying data. In fee-for-service Medicaid, state agencies adjudicate claims; in managed care, Medicaid Managed Care Organizations do. CMS receives Medicaid claims and encounter data on a lag, and the federal pre-payment analytical capacity that could plausibly support such a platform is precisely the capacity CMS dismantled. Congress is entitled to understand what data CMS actually has, how it is obtaining it, and under what legal authority, before any such platform is scaled nationally. Therefore, to assess CPI’s current compliance with Section 1936 of the Social Security Act (the Act) and the fiscal accounting of the MIP appropriation, I request the following documents and information by November 27, 2026: For each fiscal year from FY 2015 through the present, please provide the number of filled federal FTE coded exclusively to the MIP appropriation, reconciled to the 100-FTE statutory floor under Section 1936 of the Act. To the extent the workforce has fallen below the statutory floor in any fiscal year, please provide CMS’s legal justification for its noncompliance. Please provide SF-133 quarterly budget execution reports for the MIP Treasury Account Symbol for FY 2020 through FY 2025, including unobligated balances brought forward each fiscal year. Please identify any MIP-appropriated funds obligated since FY 2015 for Medicare activities, shared CMS overhead, non-Medicaid purposes, or Medicaid beneficiary eligibility verification (as distinct from the statutorily specified provider fraud and abuse purpose), together with CMS’s legal justification for those obligations under the Purpose Statute, the Anti-Deficiency Act, and the Miscellaneous Receipts Act, given that MIP is a mandatory appropriation with a specific statutory purpose. Please provide the methodology for, and actual allocation of, Unified Program Integrity Contractor costs between the MIP appropriation and Medicare appropriations from FY 2020 through the present, with Medicaid-specific deliverables identified for each fiscal year. Please provide, for each fiscal year from FY 2015 through the present, (a) MIP funds obligated to the Medicaid Integrity Institute residential training program housed at the DOJ NAC, including all deobligations and modifications of the CMS-DOJ interagency agreement, (b) actual institute expenditures by fiscal year, with a breakdown of in-person training expenditures, virtual training expenditures, and non-training expenditures (including per-class costs and number of classes offered) and (c) documentation of how funds no longer obligated for in-person training have been reallocated. Please identify any current, planned, or forecasted contract action, modification, or statement of work moving Medicaid Integrity Institute functions, including training logistics, curriculum development, state travel administration, or data analytics, to a contractor, including but not limited to GDIT. For any such action, please provide (a) the proposed and executed contract value compared to historical institute operating costs under the DOJ interagency agreement; (b) the methodology for allocating contractor labor hours and overhead between MIP-funded Medicaid-exclusive activities and HFPP funded multi-payer activities; (c) CMS’s legal analysis under the Purpose Statute, the Anti-Deficiency Act, and the Miscellaneous Receipts Act of using MIP’s Medicaid restricted mandatory appropriation to fund any multi-payer or non-Medicaid-exclusive activity; and (d) the current status of the CY 2027 MII training calendar, including whether its publication is dependent on the execution of any HFPP-related contract action. Please identify the appropriation account, funding source, staffing plan, contractor support, and Medicaid-specific deliverables of the Medicaid Fraud War Room. Please state whether any Fraud War Room resources, including, but not limited to, personnel, contract, or overhead, are drawn from the MIP appropriation, and provide the legal basis for any such allocation. Please also provide the underlying data documentation for the $203 million and 50-provider figures announced on July 28, 2026, and a breakdown of amounts actually recovered versus payments flagged, together with the underlying data documentation for the updated $342 million and 124 notices-of-intent-to-exclude figures referenced in your Deputy Administrator’s October 15, 2026 ADAPT conference presentation, and an explanation reconciling the two sets of public figures. Please describe the artificial intelligence and machine learning pilots referenced by your Deputy Administrator at the ADAPT conference on October 15, 2026, including: (a) the data sources, data flows, and legal authorities under which CMS is obtaining Medicaid claims or encounter data on a pre-payment basis in fee-for-service and managed care Medicaid; (b) the states participating in each pilot and the terms of their participation, including the Indiana-Oracle pilot and the five additional state pilots referenced; (c) the contractor(s) supporting each pilot and the acquisition vehicle(s) under which they were engaged; (d) the appropriation account(s) funding each pilot, including whether any MIP appropriated funds are being used; (e) the privacy, data security, and HIPAA frameworks governing CMS’s collection and use of pre-payment Medicaid claims and encounter data; and (f) the relationship, if any, between the pilots’ data architecture and the direct state MMIS data feeds maintained by the Division of Fraud Research and Detection prior to its elimination. Please explain how the President’s FY 2027 Budget submission treats the MIP appropriation, the Medicaid Integrity Institute, and the Section 1936 workforce, training, and technical assistance mandates, and state CMS’s position on statutory compliance in the current and coming fiscal years. Please provide all internal analyses, contractor deliverables, and data sources supporting (a) the 5 million people with personal care services figure cited in your April 2026 letter to New York Governor Kathy Hochul, (b) the alleged noncompliance related to the withholding action against Minnesota including the analytical and evidentiary basis, (c) all federal payment deferrals imposed against Minnesota, including the analytical and evidentiary basis for each deferral, (d) all federal payment deferrals imposed against California, including the analytical and evidentiary basis for each deferral, and (e) CPI’s role, if any, in supporting the HHS OIG process leading to the decertification of Hawaii and New York’s respective MFCUs. I also request a staff-level briefing within two weeks on CPI’s current compliance with Section 1936 of the Act and the operational and fiscal relationship among the MIP, the Medicaid Fraud War Room, and the Healthcare Fraud Prevention Partnership. Medicaid serves more than 73 million Americans. Program integrity in a program of that scale demands sustained investment, deep expertise, and genuine partnership with states. Congress created and funded the infrastructure to do this work, and the administration and CMS are required by law to carry out those mandates. CMS is not free to redirect the funding, redefine the mission, or replace true program integrity with a flashy, politicized rebrand. ###

Washington, D.C. – As the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) moves to clear the way for AT&T to discontinue landline services essential to Californians, U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and U.S. Representatives Doris Matsui (D-Calif.-07), Jimmy Panetta (D-Calif.-19) and Mike Thompson (D-Calif.-04) are pushing the FCC to drop this effort that will prevent California from ensuring vulnerable and rural communities have reliable landline phone service. This new inquiry follows a July 2026 letter the lawmakers sent to the FCC Chairman Brendan Carr urging him to stop AT&T from shutting down landline services; however, rather than address the lawmakers’ concerns, the FCC approved AT&T’s application to decommission approximately 360 wire centers in California. On October 30, the FCC issued a draft order to preempt California’s carrier of last resort (COLR) rules – the exact issue the lawmakers warned about. If the FCC adopts this order, it will eliminate California’s ability to require proof that wireless or fiber replacements actually work before copper wires are discontinued. It will also allow AT&T to discontinue landline service at several hundred wire centers in the state – affecting roughly 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers in rural areas in California. “These rules require telecommunications companies to provide basic phone service to anyone within their service area who requests it, ensuring that no Californian is left without access to essential communications services, including 911,” the lawmakers wrote. While the transition from copper to fiber optic systems and other technologies will modernize communications systems, the lawmakers emphasize the need to ensure service reliability and accessibility for communities. “We urge you to provide the public with sufficient time and a fair opportunity to review and weigh in on the full text of the order, rather than rush through a final decision that undermines public trust…We share the Commission’s goal in modernizing our nation’s communications networks and expanding fiber-optic infrastructure to underserved communities. However, these efforts must be executed carefully, in a manner that protects vulnerable communities during emergencies and outages and preserves universal telephone service for all Americans,” the lawmakers concluded. The full text of the letter can be found here and below. Dear Chairman Carr: We write again to raise concern over the Federal Communications Commission’s (FCC) efforts to eliminate California’s legal authority to require carriers to verify that wireless or fiber replacements function properly before retiring copper telephone networks. The draft order you circulated to the Commission on October 30, 2026, purports to preempt the California Public Utilities Commission’s (CPUC) Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules. These rules require telecommunications companies to provide basic phone service to anyone within their service area who requests it, ensuring that no Californian is left without access to essential communications services, including 911. On July 22, 2026, twenty-eight members of the California Congressional delegation asked the Commission to deny AT&T’s petitions, and that request still stands. Following that letter, the Commission approved AT&T’s application to decommission approximately 360 wire centers in California covering about 184,000 residential locations in California. If the FCC issues this purported blanket preemption, it will take away any oversight ability of California and other states to make sure sufficient alternative service exists without putting any system in place at the federal level to make that determination. In March, the Commission replaced its adequate replacement test with a carrier certification that a replacement service is available. The FCC relies on coverage reported by carriers and does not independently verify that there is alternative functioning service in the areas where copper will be retired. Without verification or oversight, California residents, including those in High Fire Threat Districts, will continue to lose basic service without access to an adequate replacement. It should be noted that California’s rules do not stand in the way of modernization and are not meant to relegate Californians to outdated technology. The CPUC has told the FCC that its rules require reliable minimum service but do not require that service to be delivered over copper. If carriers can provide a replacement that meets California’s reliability standards, nothing prevents them from retiring copper systems. Congress preserved this protection in Section 253(b) of the Communications Act to allow states to create any necessary requirements to protect public safety, safeguard consumers’ rights, and ensure the continued quality of telecommunications services. This month, the Commission is allowing copper retirement to begin in eighteen states – Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, and Wisconsin. Those customers’ experiences over time may be helpful in determining the adequacy of wireless replacements. However, there is no dedicated mechanism for consumers to report problems with replacement service after discontinuance. These problems could range from thousands of blocked calls to 911 to problems with TTY devices, medical alert systems, or home alarms. Rural communities and elderly populations will be most at risk. We urge you to provide the public with sufficient time and a fair opportunity to review and weigh in on the full text of the order, rather than rush through a final decision that undermines public trust. As carriers migrate their networks from copper to fiber optic systems and other technologies, this transition brings new opportunities to modernize our communications systems. At the same time, it raises serious questions about service reliability and accessibility, especially in areas prone to natural disasters, which increasingly extends well beyond California. The Commission recognized these concerns in September when it pulled another discontinuance application from automatic approval for further review, and it should apply the same level of scrutiny in this circumstance. At the very least, any order should carve out areas at high risk for fires and other natural disasters and areas without verified indoor cellular coverage. We also request that you respond in writing to the following questions by December 15, 2026, and before any vote on the draft order: Should a carrier have to show, with independently verified data, that its replacement service provides reliable indoor coverage before retiring copper in high-fire-threat areas? If not, what showing should be required? Of the more than 184,000 California locations approved for discontinuance, how many are in High Fire Threat Districts, and how many lack indoor wireless coverage? Do you agree that demonstrating wireless coverage under normal operating conditions does not necessarily establish that a network will remain reliable during a wildfire, extended power outage, or other natural disaster? If testing identifies locations where the replacement service is unreliable or unavailable, will the FCC require the carrier to maintain existing service until an adequate alternative is available? Many wireless services stop working when the power goes out. Will the FCC require backup power for replacement services in disaster-prone areas so customers can still call 911 during outages? For customers in states approved for copper retirement, what mechanisms will be available to those individuals to report service failures, and how will the FCC use those reports? Should a state be permitted to require a carrier to demonstrate that its replacement service is reliable before landline service is discontinued? Should a federal discontinuance authorization automatically override state public safety requirements that address risks the FCC did not evaluate rigorously? Why should the Commission act before the courts rule on the challenges to the Network Modernization Order? Will the FCC share outage reporting data with state commissions, local governments, and first responders, with any necessary confidentiality safeguards applied to the data? We share the Commission’s goal in modernizing our nation’s communications networks and expanding fiber-optic infrastructure to underserved communities. However, these efforts must be executed carefully, in a manner that protects vulnerable communities during emergencies and outages and preserves universal telephone service for all Americans. ###

Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), a member of the Senate Agriculture Committee, and other Senate Democrats are calling out Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Chair Michael Selig for the agency’s decision to prohibit prediction markets from geofencing, effectively requiring prediction markets to offer contracts in all 50 states and Tribal lands. The Senators note Selig’s action directly conflicts with active court orders in California, Michigan, Nevada and Washington – and demand that he reverse it. “Numerous courts have held that sports-related event contracts are not swaps and instead are indistinguishable from sports bets subject to state and tribal gaming laws…. The courts have ordered platforms to cease offering various prediction contracts in Michigan, Nevada, and Washington, and on the land of two California tribes, and imposed geofencing requirements. The Commission now appears to be encouraging prediction markets to offer prohibited contracts in contempt of these court orders during active litigation,” the Senators wrote. “We are particularly troubled that this action came just hours after the Northern District of California issued its latest court order in Blue Lake Rancheria v. Kalshi requiring Kalshi to geofence around the plaintiff’s tribal lands. This interpretation raises concerns that the Commission may be coordinating with platforms currently engaged in litigation and encouraging them to violate state and tribal gaming laws… The Commission must withdraw the interpretation or freeze all efforts to implement until litigation is resolved.” the Senators continued. Joining Schiff are all Senators representing California, Michigan, Nevada and Washington, Senators Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.), Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), Patty Murray (D-Wash.), Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), Gary Peters (D-Mich.) and Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), as well as the Ranking Member of the Senate Agriculture Committee Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.). The full text of the letter can be found here and below: Dear Chairman Selig: We write to express our opposition to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s November 5 interpretation ordering Designated Contract Markets (DCMs) to end access criteria that restrict access to certain event contract markets based on prospective traders’ location or residence (e.g., geofencing) within 30 days. Your unilateral decision directly conflicts with active court orders, undermines state and tribal law, and must be reversed. Numerous courts have held that sports-related event contracts are not swaps and instead are indistinguishable from sports bets subject to state and tribal gaming laws. Your novel interpretation of the impartial access requirements effectively requires DCMs to offer improperly regulated gambling products in all fifty states without regard to state and tribal gaming laws and these state and federal court decisions. There is no basis or precedent under 17 CFR 38.151(b)’s impartial access requirements for this interpretation and indeed this argument has been made in several of the active cases—and rejected. The Sixth and Ninth Circuits have ruled that states retain the authority to apply state gaming laws to prediction markets. The Ninth Circuit has also ruled that sports event contracts on Tribal lands constitute unauthorized Class III gaming under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act in the preliminary-injunction context. The courts have ordered platforms to cease offering various prediction contracts in Michigan, Nevada, and Washington, and on the land of two California tribes, and imposed geofencing requirements. The Commission now appears to be encouraging prediction markets to offer prohibited contracts in contempt of these court orders during active litigation. We are particularly troubled that this action came just hours after the Northern District of California issued its latest court order in Blue Lake Rancheria v. Kalshi requiring Kalshi to geofence around the plaintiff’s tribal lands. This interpretation raises concerns that the Commission may be coordinating with platforms currently engaged in litigation and encouraging them to violate state and tribal gaming laws. The Commission must withdraw the interpretation or freeze all efforts to implement until litigation is resolved. At minimum, the Commission must expressly state that the following do not violate Regulation 38.151(b): geographic restrictions imposed by court order, those adopted to comply with the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act or tribal-state compacts, and those an exchange adopts voluntarily. We further request that the Commission preserve all records and communications relating to the topics addressed in this letter, from January 1, 2025, to the present and continue preserving existing and future materials on an ongoing basis. This preservation hold applies to all relevant records within the Commission’s possession and any person or entity representing or purporting to be acting on its behalf. This includes, but is not limited to, records and communications via email, whether official or personal; mobile devices; encrypted or disappearing messaging applications; social media; calendar entries; meeting notes; and voicemail and text messages. To the extent that the Commission uses any auto-delete functions, it should immediately suspend auto-delete functions and notify persons with control over potentially relevant records of similar preservation obligations. Thank you for your attention to this matter. We look forward to your prompt response by November 23, 2026, including a written confirmation that the Commission is preserving all records related to this Congressional inquiry. ###

Lawmakers warn administration’s changes would leave protected species vulnerable to foreseeable deaths and habitat destruction Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), member of the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works and Ranking Member of the Fisheries, Water, and Wildlife Subcommittee; U.S. Representatives Jared Huffman (D-Calif.-02), House Natural Resources Committee Ranking Member; Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.-06) and Don Beyer (D-Va.-08); and U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Ranking Member on the Senate Committee on Environment & Public Works, led 37 other Democratic lawmakers in demanding answers from Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on the Trump administration’s attempts to gut core Endangered Species Act (ESA) protections by reinterpreting what the agencies consider “incidental take” and “harm” in memoranda to federal employees. The lawmakers warned the reinterpretation would strip protections from wildlife killed or injured by otherwise lawful activities, even when those deaths and injuries could be foreseen. Under the administration’s interpretation, the law’s prohibition on killing or injuring protected wildlife would apply only when someone deliberately targets a protected species. The lawmakers warned this would undermine decades of safeguards that allow economic activity to proceed while requiring commonsense steps to prevent wildlife deaths and injuries. “For decades, the ESA has provided a framework for allowing economic activity to proceed while requiring reasonable measures to avoid and minimize harm to threatened and endangered species. These memoranda would undermine that framework by removing incentives to prevent foreseeable wildlife deaths and injuries,” the lawmakers wrote. The letter challenges two identical internal memos issued September 14 by U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Director Brian Nesvik and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration General Counsel John Luce. The memos direct staff to interpret “take” — which includes killing or injuring protected wildlife — as covering only intentional actions targeting those animals. The lawmakers are demanding an explanation of the legal basis for that interpretation and whether activities that could foreseeably kill or injure endangered species still require permits. The directives came as the Trump administration eliminated the longstanding regulatory definition of “harm,” which covered habitat destruction that kills or injures protected wildlife. Both changes took effect the same day, threatening protections for endangered animals and the places they need to survive. “Any reinterpretation that could eliminate protections for these species is a serious and troubling departure from that framework and would undermine the law’s implementation,” the lawmakers wrote. The lawmakers requested responses by November 30, 2026, including what protections would remain for species threatened by habitat destruction and whether states and Tribes were consulted. They also asked whether Interior would suspend implementation until it publicly explains its legal reasoning and assesses the consequences for endangered wildlife. “The Services must abandon this approach and preserve the ESA’s longstanding protections for threatened and endangered wildlife and the communities that depend on them,” the lawmakers concluded. Additional House signers included Representatives Becca Balint (D-Vt.), Suzanne Bonamici (D-Ore.), Julia Brownley (D-Calif.), Ed Case (D-Hawai’i), Steve Cohen (D-Tenn.), Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas), Diana DeGette (D-Colo.), Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.), Sarah Elfreth (D-Md.), Dwight Evans (D-Pa.), Glenn Ivey (D-Md.), Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.), Mike Levin (D-Calif.), Sarah McBride (D-Del.), Dave Min (D-Calif.), Kevin Mullin (D-Calif.), Frank Pallone Jr. (D-N.J.), Scott Peters (D-Calif.), Emily Randall (D-Wash.), Deborah Ross (D-N.C.), Mary Gay Scanlon (D-Pa.), Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.), Dina Titus (D-Nev.), Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.), Jill Tokuda (D-Hawai’i), and Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Fla.). Additional Senate signers included Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Mazie Hirono (D-Hawai’i), Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.), Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Jack Reed (D-R.I.), Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), and Ron Wyden (D-Ore.). Background: Recently, Senators Schiff and Whitehouse introduced a privileged resolution to reject the administration’s unprecedented attempt to circumvent Congress’s intent when it passed the Endangered Species Act in 1973 and to stop the reversal of a decades-old provision meant to protect our wildlife. The Senators will force a vote in the coming weeks. The full text of the letter can be found here and below. Dear Secretary Burgum and Secretary Lutnick: We write in strong opposition to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s (FWS’s) and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s (NOAA’s) – (“the Services”) unlawful reinterpretation of “harm” and “take” in the Endangered Species Act (ESA). In two internal memoranda to staff released on September 14, 2026 – one issued by the FWS Director Brian Nesvik and another from NOAA General Counsel John Luce – the Services reinterpret settled law regarding protections for threatened and endangered wildlife under the ESA. The ESA is one of America’s most successful and widely supported environmental laws. The memoranda reinterpret unlawful “take” under the ESA to only include intentional actions targeting threatened and endangered species. Under this interpretation, incidental killing, injury, or other forms of take resulting from otherwise lawful activities would fall outside the ESA’s protections. With nearly a third of America’s wildlife at risk of extinction, we should bolster our efforts to protect threatened and endangered species, not weaken them. This reinterpretation raises concerns about the future of the ESA’s incidental take permitting system. For decades, the ESA has provided a framework for allowing economic activity to proceed while requiring reasonable measures to avoid and minimize harm to threatened and endangered species. These memoranda would undermine that framework by removing incentives to prevent foreseeable wildlife deaths and injuries. This illegal reinterpretation of take, combined with the Department of the Interior (DOI) and the Department of Commerce (DOC) rule rescinding the regulatory definition of “harm” under the ESA, which went into effect on September 14, 2026, would render Section 9 prohibitions hollow, in essence only preventing purposeful take of an animal. Until September, the Services had long recognized that significant habitat modification or degradation could constitute “harm” because it could have indirect impacts on the survival of an animal. These new memoranda attempt to entirely eliminate any guardrails on incidental take. We have worked in Congress to safeguard the ESA and ensure federal agencies carry out their duty under the ESA to prevent extinction and recover species. We are alarmed by the enormous consequences the interpretation could have for species across the country. To better understand the Services’ position and assist the oversight of the House Natural Resources Committee and the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, please respond to the following questions by November 30, 2026: Do the September 14, 2026 memoranda represent the official legal position of DOI and the DOC? If so, when did it take effect, and what legal guidance did DOC and DOI issue to field offices regarding its implementation? What statutory language and legal precedent support the memoranda’s conclusion that incidental killing or injury of endangered species does not constitute a prohibited “take” unless the activity was specifically intended to target the animal? How do DOI and DOC reconcile the new interpretation with the Supreme Court’s decision in Babbitt, which upheld the inclusion of habitat modification that kills or injures protected wildlife within the ESA’s definition of “harm”? Do DOI and DOC continue to require incidental take permits for activities that may foreseeably kill or injure endangered species? If the memorandum changes those requirements, please describe how. What protections would remain available for endangered species whose threats involve incidental take, including incidental harm and habitat destruction, from otherwise lawful activities? Did DOI and DOC consult with states, Tribes, or other relevant stakeholders before issuing or distributing the memorandum? If so, please describe the nature and timeline of such consultations. Will DOI suspend implementation of the memorandum pending a public explanation of its legal basis and an assessment of its implications on the ESA? The ESA has provided a framework for protecting endangered wildlife while allowing economic activity to continue with appropriate safeguards for over 50 years. Any reinterpretation that could eliminate protections for these species is a serious and troubling departure from that framework and would undermine the law’s implementation. The Services must abandon this approach and preserve the ESA’s longstanding protections for threatened and endangered wildlife and the communities that depend on them. Please contact the Natural Resources Committee Subcommittee on Water, Wildlife and Fisheries minority staff at (202) 225-6065 with any questions about this request. We look forward to your prompt response to this oversight request. ###

Washington, D.C. – This week, the U.S. Senate unanimously passed U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.)’s legislation to begin the process to designate the Bay Area Ridge Trail as a National Scenic Trail. This designation would enhance the trail’s visibility as a world-class recreation opportunity and attract new visitors, in addition to helping connect the different routes within the trail. “The Bay Area Ridge Trail gives visitors to the Bay Area and its residents the opportunity to enjoy more than 500 miles of some of California’s most incredible outdoor beauty, including parks and preserves. Providing federal recognition to this ridgeline trail will help preserve it for future generations. I am proud to continue working with federal and local partners to get this across the finish line,” said Senator Schiff. “The Bay Area Ridge Trail is a crown jewel of our region, providing millions of people with access to some of the most stunning natural landscapes in the country and connecting our communities to the outdoors,” said Representative Huffman. “Designating it as a National Scenic Trail would not only help complete it – it would set it on par with iconic trails like the Appalachian and Pacific Crest and elevate the incredible and diverse Bay Area landscapes. This would be a major boost for the recreation economy, and our bill gets that ball rolling. I’m grateful to my partners in the Senate for moving our bill forward and am excited to get it across the finish line.” “The Bay Area Ridge Trail is one of Northern California’s many treasures, connecting local communities and visitors to historic and breathtaking landscapes that make our state so special,” said Senator Padilla. “This is an important step toward designating it as a National Scenic Trail in order to safeguard our public lands, strengthen conservation efforts, and bolster our tourism economy. I’m proud to work alongside my colleagues and see our bill pass the Senate, ensuring Californians and visitors alike have access to our extraordinary outdoor recreation opportunities.” The legislation requires the National Park Service to complete the required feasibility study in consultation with the Bay Area Ridge Trail Council and relevant federal, state, and tribal agencies. The trail meets all the required criteria established in the National Trails System Act of 1968 for National Scenic Trail designation, including: Extended trail route of more than 100 miles Provides maximum outdoor recreation potential Provides for enjoyment of nationally significant scenic, historic, and cultural qualities Represents desert, marsh, grassland, mountain, canyon, river, and forest Represents landforms that exhibit significant regional geographic characteristics Connects with side trails, which provide additional public access The legislation is led by U.S. Representative Jared Huffman (D-Calif.-02) in the House, and is cosponsored by U.S. Senator Alex Padilla and every member of the Bay Area delegation. The full text of the legislation is available here. ###

Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), a member of the Senate Agriculture Committee, and Senator Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.) are leading Senators in pressing Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Chairman Selig for answers on reporting that the CFTC sought to retract an investigative referral into potential insider trading. Minutes before President Trump backed away from threats to strike Iranian power plants on March 23, billions of dollars worth of contracts were placed predicting oil would fall and the S&P would rise, raising concerns about insider trading. According to reporting , CFTC political appointee Arun Mel Gunewardena directed career staff to retract a referral to the Division of Enforcement to examine the suspicious trading activity. He subsequently assembled a separate team to conduct a new analysis of the trading activity, reportedly excluding the CFTC’s career analysts who prepared the original referral. “Mr. Gunewardena’s reported intervention raises urgent concerns that political leadership may have interfered with career staff’s efforts to investigate potentially unlawful trading, compromising the independence and integrity of the CFTC’s enforcement process. For months, many of us have urged you to investigate a spate of suspicious trades in oil markets, totaling billions of dollars,” the Senators wrote. “The CFTC has a statutory authority promoting the integrity of America’s commodity futures and derivatives markets and has significant enforcement authorities to punish wrongdoing. Since President Trump’s second inauguration, the CFTC has already seen an exodus of both senior career Division of Enforcement leadership and staff attorneys. Public reporting also indicates that the number of CFTC enforcement actions has declined substantially compared with previous fiscal years,” the Senators continued. The Senators are requesting the CFTC provide answers on whether the agency was made aware that a referral of suspicious trading had been made, the communications between Mr. Gunewardena and career staff, the CFTC’s procedure to refer, evaluate, and investigate suspected insider trading, what precedent, if any, is there for a political appointee or other senior level CFTC official to direct the retraction of an enforcement referral, and what assurances that enforcement determinations will be made independently by enforcement staff without inappropriate interference from political appointees. They’re also urging the agency to preserve all records and communications relating to the topics addressed. In addition to Schiff and Warnock, this letter is signed by Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), Michael Bennet (D-Colo), Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), Jack Reed (D-R.I.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.). The full text of the letter is available here and below: Dear Chairman Selig, We write seeking answers about public reporting that Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) political appointee Arun Mel Gunewardena sought to “retract” an investigative referral into billions of dollars of highly suspicious trading that occurred just minutes before President Trump backtracked on threats against Iran. In May 2026, many of us wrote to you urging the CFTC to conduct a “swift and thorough” investigation into suspicious oil futures trading ahead of major announcements of U.S. military operations concerning Iran. To date, we have not received a response to that request. Mr. Gunewardena’s reported intervention raises urgent concerns that political leadership may have interfered with career staff’s efforts to investigate potentially unlawful trading, compromising the independence and integrity of the CFTC’s enforcement process. For months, many of us have urged you to investigate a spate of suspicious trades in oil markets, totaling billions of dollars. One incident in particular that we urged the CFTC to investigate involved hundreds of millions in trading shortly before President Trump’s March 23, 2026, post on Truth Social that indicated negotiations with Iran had progressed over the weekend and there would be a postponement of strikes for five days. According to public reporting, CFTC staff examined the suspicious trading activity and determined that a referral to the Division of Enforcement was warranted. However, Mr. Gunewardena, a political appointee who joined the CFTC on March 2, 2026, reportedly directed career staff to retract the referral. He subsequently assembled a separate team to conduct a new analysis of the trading activity, reportedly excluding the CFTC’s career analysts who prepared the original referral. The CFTC has a statutory authority promoting the integrity of America’s commodity futures and derivatives markets and has significant enforcement authorities to punish wrongdoing. Since President Trump’s second inauguration, the CFTC has already seen an exodus of both senior career Division of Enforcement leadership and staff attorneys. Public reporting also indicates that the number of CFTC enforcement actions has declined substantially compared with previous fiscal years. Mr. Gunewardena’s actions raise additional serious questions about whether political appointees have improperly influenced the CFTC’s handling of suspicious trading activity and whether such intervention has affected the independence or effectiveness of ongoing enforcement investigations. Accordingly, we respectfully request that the Commission provide written responses to the following questions no later than November 23, 2026: Were you aware of these trades prior to the publishing of the October 13, 2026, Bloomberg article “CFTC Staff Told to Retract Analysis of Suspicious Oil Trades”? When were you made aware that a referral of suspicious trading had been made? Did you participate in any meetings or calls related to the trades referenced in the article? When were you made aware that Mr. Gunewardena had sought to retract the referral? Was the referral subsequently withdrawn or modified, and if so, when and at whose direction? How did Mr. Gunewardena communicate with CFTC career staff to retract the referral of suspicious trading related to the conflict with Iran? If in writing, please produce copies of all records of Mr. Gunewardena’s request and related communications involving CFTC employees. Please also produce the original referral to the Division of Enforcement, any subsequent amendments or withdrawal instructions, and communications concerning the decision to conduct a separate analysis of the trading activity. Did you discuss this issue with Mr. Gunewardena or any other CFTC officials prior to Mr. Gunewardena’s actions to retract the referral? Public reporting indicates that CFTC leadership determined a broader review of the trading activity was warranted, including examination of additional domestic and international markets. Why would expanding the scope of that review require withdrawing or modifying the original referral to the Division of Enforcement, rather than supplementing the existing referral? Who made that determination, and what was the basis for it? What is CFTC’s procedure to refer, evaluate, and investigate suspected violations of the Commodity Exchange Act and related regulations, including insider trading? What precedent, if any, is there for a political appointee or other senior level CFTC official to direct the retraction of an enforcement referral? How many times has a CFTC political or other senior level CFTC official sought to retract, modify, or otherwise intervene in a referral filed with the Division of Enforcement? What standards are used to assess whether such a retraction is appropriate or runs afoul of federal ethics laws or CFTC’s procedures? Is CFTC conducting an internal review or investigation of this reported intervention by a political appointee? What steps is CFTC taking to determine whether Mr. Gunewardena’s reported intervention complied with agency policies, procedures, and applicable ethics requirements? What corrective actions, if any, have been taken? What assurances can you provide that enforcement determinations will be made independently by enforcement staff, without inappropriate interference from political appointees? Is the Division of Enforcement investigating the suspicious trades at issue? a. Is there any information that you can share about the status of that investigation? b. Did Mr. Gunewardena’s reported intervention delay, narrow, suspend, or otherwise affect the Division of Enforcement’s investigation? c. Does the Division of Enforcement retain access to the original referral, supporting trading data, and analysis prepared by career Market Oversight staff? d. What steps is the CFTC taking to ensure that the investigation proceeds independently and without undue delay? This information and these records are needed for the Senate to exercise its essential oversight and legislative functions. We further request that the Commission preserve all records and communications relating to the topics addressed in this letter, from January 1, 2025, to the present and continue preserving such materials on an ongoing basis. This includes, but is not limited to, records and communications via email, whether official or personal; mobile devices; encrypted or disappearing messaging applications; social media; calendar entries; meeting notes; and voicemail and text messages. To the extent that the Commission uses any auto-delete functions, it should immediately suspend auto-delete functions and notify persons with control over potentially relevant records of similar preservation obligations.
