Schiff: “ The cruelty is the policy, and we need to put a stop to it.” San Diego, CA – Last week, U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) joined members of the U.S. House of Representatives San Diego delegation Sara Jacobs (D-Calif.-51), Scott Peters (D-Calif.-50), Juan Vargas (D-Calif.-52) and Mike Levin (D-Calif.-49) for a press conference raising the alarm about the Trump administration’s increased ICE enforcement actions in San Diego communities. At Point Loma High School, Schiff and his colleagues called for an end to the administration’s cruel and unusual practices, including immigration enforcement at schools and promised increased oversight should the Congressional majority flip in the midterm elections. The Senator’s visit marks San Diego Unified School District’s first visit from a sitting U.S. Senator in 13 years. The press conference followed an assembly where Schiff spoke to students about the importance of civic participation and answered questions on a range of topics. Key Excerpts: On increased ICE enforcement actions taking place in San Diego: […] We are working hard, my colleagues and I to push back on those ICE operations and make sure we keep them away from schools and other places that ought to be a sanctuary, like religious institutions or bus stops, hospitals […] We’ve only seen this problem grow worse in the last few months, and it was terrible to begin with. No one should have to worry about going to school, getting an education. Their parents shouldn’t have to worry about dropping them off at school. This ought to be a place of learning and safety for all of our students, and I appreciate all you’re doing, Superintendent, to make that so. On a recent incident at Marshall Elementary School in Chollas Creek involving children aged 2 and 5 years-old: […] One of the most heartbreaking stories comes right out of San Diego, and that is two parents dropping off two young children, and then being arrested and detained, without ICE even making any kind of provision, giving any thought to what happens to those young children. What was supposed to happen to them after school that day? Were they supposed to go to be picked up and wait for their parents to never arrive? Sadly, the whole point of how they are administering immigration policy is the cruelty. The cruelty is the policy, and we need to put a stop to it. I’m proud to sponsor a couple bills designed to try to prevent schools from becoming a fulcrum of immigration enforcement. One, the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act, I’m proud to co-sponsor, that would place schools and school busses, places of worship, and hospitals and other sensitive locations, by statute, off limits for ICE enforcement actions. Another that I’ve introduced, the Fairness to Freedom Act, would provide a right to counsel for people who cannot afford it otherwise, facing a deportation or a serious immigration case. These will help if we’re successful in getting them passed. Of course, we can’t get them passed in this Congress, but if the majority changes hands in 19 days, we’ll have an opportunity to pass bills like these and like others that my colleagues are supporting. […] There needs to be oversight here, and there’s been virtually no oversight. None of us chair any of the relevant committees in the minority, and our colleagues in the majority have been unwilling to ask the hard questions because they don’t want to know the answers. We’re shocked, and we should be shocked, by those ages two and five. I mean, who does that? And the thing of it is that this is all being done in our names. This is the U.S. government. This is being done in our names, and I’m sick of it. It’s grotesque, and it has to stop. And if we don’t have the votes to stop it right now, I sure as hell hope we do shortly, because we can’t keep operating this way. We’re a better country than this. We’re a more decent people than this. On what Americans can expect from the Trump administration in the lead up to and aftermath of the midterm elections: […] I think we can expect his actions to become only more and more erratic. They were erratic to begin with, but I think when you compare Trump two to Trump one, it is a whole order of magnitude worse, and it’s not getting better during Trump two. So, I think we are all deeply concerned by just how cruel, erratic, norm-shattering, law-breaking, corrupt this President and White House have become. To the point of advocating public executions, to the point of having Russian oligarchs pay for wedding parties, to the point of people contributing to the ballroom, getting pardons and special government contracts. It’s grotesque. It’s grotesque, and one of the things that I’m looking forward to is having a chance to finally do oversight and put in place not just norms anymore, which apparently can be trampled, but laws that have teeth, so we can prevent this kind of conduct from ever happening again. ###

Washington, D.C. — U.S. Senators Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), Chris Murphy (D-Conn.), and Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) on Friday led in a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche demanding answers on the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) decision to break with decades of precedent and unilaterally refuse to enforce a prohibition against the sale of handguns to people under the age of 21. Schiff, Murphy, and Kelly also fought back against these ATF rule changes through the rulemaking comment process. The Senators highlighted the enormous risks to public safety if handguns are placed in teens’ hands: “The public safety implications of this decision are clear. Numerous mass shootings have been committed by perpetrators between the ages of 18 and 20, including the shooting at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, where an 18-year-old fatally shot 19 students and two teachers and injured 18 others, as well as the shootings at a supermarket in Buffalo, New York; an Indianapolis FedEx facility and Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida. These tragic examples underscore the public safety considerations at stake and the serious risks Congress sought to address.” The Senators laid out the decades-long, bipartisan consensus on banning gun dealers from selling firearms to teenagers: “Congress enacted this prohibition as part of the Gun Control Act of 1968, clearly stating that ‘it shall be unlawful’ for an FFL to sell or transfer a handgun to a person under age 21. Nearly 60 years later, the Department’s decision to stop enforcing this provision comes not because Congress repealed or amended the law, but because the Executive Branch has independently concluded that these provisions are unconstitutional. This decision raises serious questions about the Department’s execution of federal law, its communications with members of the gun industry, and the implications for the enforcement of federal firearms laws nationwide.” The Senators argued Blanche’s decision is another authoritarian power grab over the judicial branch and Congress: “The Department’s OLC opinion acknowledges the constitutionality of age-based firearms restrictions has ‘deeply divided members of the federal bench.’ Given the ongoing nature of this legal dispute, the Department’s decision that it may cease enforcement of federal law by executive fiat, rather than continue defending and enforcing the statute, represents an expansive and concerning assertion of executive authority.” The Senators concluded by requesting Blanche provide the following information on the authority and research supporting his decision: A detailed explanation of the legal authority on which the Department relies to stop criminal and civil enforcement of these provisions, despite their continued status as federal law; All legal materials concerning the Department’s decision to stop enforcing 18 U.S.C. § 922(b)(1) and (c)(1) against federally licensed firearm dealers that sell handguns to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20; Any analysis conducted or reviewed by the Department regarding the potential public-safety consequences of changing federal enforcement policy for handgun sales to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20; and A list of all investigations, prosecutions, and civil or criminal enforcement actions affected by the Department’s decision, including any matters declined, suspended, dismissed, or otherwise modified, and the reasons for each action. Schiff, Murphy, and Kelly were joined by U.S. Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.), Cory Booker (D-N.J.), Chris Coons (D-Del.), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii), Tim Kaine (D-Va.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.), Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), Ed Markey (D-Mass.), Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Jack Reed (D-R.I.), Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Peter Welch (D-Vt.), and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.). A full transcript of the letter is available below. A copy of the letter is available here . Dear Attorney General Blanche: We write regarding the U.S. Department of Justice’s (the Department) decision to cease enforcement of longstanding federal restrictions on the sale of handguns to individuals under the age of 21 by federally licensed firearms dealers (FFLs). This significant change in federal enforcement policy raises serious questions about the Department’s legal justification, and we request information regarding the analysis underlying its decision. On September 18, 2026, the Department’s Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) published a legal opinion concluding that 18 U.S.C. § 922(b)(1) and (c)(1)—the federal prohibition on FFLs selling handguns to 18- to 20-year-olds—violate the Second Amendment, and that federal prosecutors may no longer prosecute FFLs that sell handguns to 18- to 20-year-olds who are not otherwise prohibited from gun possession. [1] Congress enacted this prohibition as part of the Gun Control Act of 1968, clearly stating that “it shall be unlawful” for an FFL to sell or transfer a handgun to a person under age 21. [2] Nearly 60 years later, the Department’s decision to stop enforcing this provision comes not because Congress repealed or amended the law, but because the Executive Branch has independently concluded that these provisions are unconstitutional. This decision raises serious questions about the Department’s execution of federal law, its communications with members of the gun industry, and the implications for the enforcement of federal firearms laws nationwide. The Department’s OLC opinion acknowledges the constitutionality of age-based firearms restrictions has “deeply divided members of the federal bench.” Given the ongoing nature of this legal dispute, the Department’s decision that it may cease enforcement of federal law by executive fiat, rather than continue defending and enforcing the statute, represents an expansive and concerning assertion of executive authority. The public safety implications of this decision are clear. Numerous mass shootings have been committed by perpetrators between the ages of 18 and 20, including the shooting at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, where an 18-year-old fatally shot 19 students and two teachers and injured 18 others, as well as the shootings at a supermarket in Buffalo, New York; an Indianapolis FedEx facility and Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida. These tragic examples underscore the public safety considerations at stake and the serious risks Congress sought to address. The Department’s decision to unilaterally cease enforcement of this provision of law raises serious questions and concerns. Thus, we request the Department provide: A detailed explanation of the legal authority on which the Department relies to stop criminal and civil enforcement of these provisions, despite their continued status as federal law; All legal materials concerning the Department’s decision to stop enforcing 18 U.S.C. § 922(b)(1) and (c)(1) against federally licensed firearm dealers that sell handguns to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20; Any analysis conducted or reviewed by the Department regarding the potential public-safety consequences of changing federal enforcement policy for handgun sales to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20; and A list of all investigations, prosecutions, and civil or criminal enforcement actions affected by the Department’s decision, including any matters declined, suspended, dismissed, or otherwise modified, and the reasons for each action. Please provide the requested information and documents by November 16, 2026. ###

Walnut Creek, CA — Today, Senators Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla (both-D-Calif.) are announcing that nearly $2.5 million is heading to public safety projects in San Francisco, Alameda, and Walnut Creek. The federal funding was secured by Senators Schiff and Padilla through the Congressionally Directed Spending process for fiscal year 2026. As a result of the Senators’ efforts, $1 million has been disbursed to the City of Walnut Creek, $900,000 has been disbursed to the City of Alameda, and $550,000 has been disbursed to the City of San Francisco for projects that will prevent crime and keep communities safe. The funding is part of more than $258,959,654 delivered by Senator Schiff since taking office. “All Californians deserve to live in communities where their families are safe and their businesses can thrive. They also deserve to have the peace of mind of knowing that when a crime does take place, local law enforcement has the tools to bring the perpetrators to justice,” said Senator Schiff. “I’m proud to have secured nearly $2.5 million in federal funding with the partnership of Senator Padilla and Congressman DeSaulnier, which is now headed to Bay Area communities, to deliver on that promise.” “Keeping our communities safe means investing in the tools and services that help prevent crime, support victims, and hold perpetrators accountable,” said Senator Padilla . “I’m proud to have secured this federal funding for Alameda and San Francisco, delivering resources that strengthen public safety and help ensure Californians get the support and protection they deserve to feel safe in their own communities.” Read more about the projects below: City of Walnut Creek Public Safety Body Worn Camera Equipment Upgrade Project The Walnut Creek Police Department has received $1,000,000 to implement their Public Safety Body Worn Camera Equipment Upgrade Project. The purpose is to provide equipment upgrades and services for the department’s Body Worn Camera (BWC) program. This project is intended to improve accountability and transparency and strengthen data collection and the preservation of digital evidence. This funding request was led by Senator Schiff and Congressman Mark DeSaulnier (D-Calif.-10). “Body-worn cameras are critical in promoting transparency, ensuring accountability, and developing public trust in police departments,” said Congressman DeSaulnier. “I was proud to bring home $1 million for the City of Walnut Creek to upgrade 120 body-worn cameras for their officers and provide cutting-edge technology for the department that will ultimately make our community safer. I am grateful for the leadership of Senators Schiff and Padilla for supporting public safety reforms statewide.” City of Alameda Crime Victims Initiative The City of Alameda City Attorney’s Office has received $900,000 in federal funding, which will sustain and expand victim services in response to rapidly increasing caseloads, particularly involving domestic violence, elder abuse, child abuse, and other misdemeanor crimes, through an embedded victim advocacy program in the Prosecution and Public Rights Unit. The project will increase access to victim services, offer greater continuity of support throughout criminal proceedings, expand service availability, improve awareness of available resources, and sustain and institutionalize a victim advocacy program that strengthens services for crime victims throughout Alameda. This funding request was led by Senator Padilla and supported by Senator Schiff. City and County of San Francisco’s Crime Lab Rapid DNA Unit The San Francisco Police Department-Crime Lab Rapid DNA Unit has received $550,000 to support efforts to acquire and implement two National DNA Index System (NDIS)-approved Rapid DNA instruments, along with the associated software, consumables, validation materials, and training required to integrate this technology into forensic operations. Rapid DNA technology automates DNA extraction, amplification, separation, and profile generation within a single instrument, reducing analysis time from weeks to less than two hours for qualifying samples. This capability will significantly improve investigative timelines, increase laboratory efficiency, and enhance the delivery of critical forensic information to investigators and criminal justice partners. This funding request was led by Senator Schiff. ###

Schiff told viewers of MS Now’s All in with Chris Hayes that voting early is their best tool in responding to attempts by the Trump administration to sow chaos in the upcoming election Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) joined MS NOW’s All in with Chris Hayes to discuss the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) lawsuit against California, the administration’s latest attempt at sowing chaos before the November elections. This week, the Los Angeles County Registrar received a thumb drive from the DOJ, which the department claimed contained a list of “likely non-citizens” that California was expected to purge from its voter rolls. The password to the thumb drive came attached via ‘Post-it’ note, and the drive was not reviewed due to security concerns. The DOJ has now sued California for failure to meet the department’s demands and deadline. Senator Schiff explained that these tactics date back to the aftermath of the 2020 election, and are engineered to generate doubt in the security of our elections. The Senator encouraged Californians to vote early as a response to these attempts to undermine faith in the upcoming midterms. View the full interview here . Key Excerpts: On why the DOJ has lawlessly targeted California’s elections ahead of the midterms: […] They know at the Department of Justice because it’s run by one of the president’s criminal lawyers that the president is losing these Midterms badly. He has not brought the cost of living down. His war is unpopular. His tariff war is unpopular. And so, they are using any stratagem they can to try to suppress the vote, to change the vote. And now you have this desperate action in California, where they want California to take some random thumb drive and run it through their system. On this administration’s previous attempts at election interference and the validity of current claims: […] But where this has been tried in other states like in Nevada, the Justice Department, administration, initially claimed that there were 10,000-20,000 ballots of non-citizens and then revised the estimate down to well, maybe more like 100 or 200. The number turned out to be zero. Zero. But I think bigger picture, Chris, they want to cast these doubts now. They assume they will lose this litigation in the run-up to the election so that after the election, if and when they lose, they can try to contest the results. […] The feds have very limited role when it comes to elections. That is the province of the states. They lose time after time after time. The civil rights division, which is now the anti-civil rights division, has brought some of these cases. They’ve lost them all. I think they expect to lose this one, too. But nevertheless, you have the Attorney General of the United States soiling the name of that office, soiling his own reputation to put the department’s imprimatur on this disenfranchisement, voter disenfranchisement effort. It’s just scandalous, but thankfully such an incompetent effort. On what can be done to secure the 2026 elections: […] The President in his last term claimed there were millions of undocumented people voting in California. That was a bigger lie, but it’s still all part of the same big lie. So, they might contest seating someone. They might use it as justification to seize ballot boxes. One concern I have is, they’re dispatching all kinds of poll watchers from the Justice Department, from the Civil Rights Division. There are going to be legitimate poll watchers out there. It wouldn’t be difficult to seed the crowd with outside agitators, create violent incidents to give the administration some pretext to call out the guard or call out ICE or call out whoever. The best response in California is vote early, vote by absentee. We’re all mailed a ballot in California where that’s possible, but other states people should vote early if they can. But also, I think people should look at every effort this administration makes to tell them, we don’t want people voting — we don’t want citizens voting, because we’re afraid of losing. We should look at all those efforts to stop people from voting and make it even more of a mission to vote and make sure your voice is heard. ###

Lawmakers Reject Kirkland’s Excuses for Stonewalling Investigation and Demand Immediate Compliance Washington, D.C. —Today, U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) joined Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.-08), Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee and Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Ranking Member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations to press Chairman of the law firm Kirkland & Ellis Jon Ballis on refusing to cooperate with the Committees’ investigation into Kirkland’s decision to provide President Trump with $125 million in free legal services that align with his political agenda – rejecting the firm’s previous bogus legal justifications for doing so. “To date, Kirkland has not cooperated with our legitimate oversight requests. Your firm has failed to produce a single responsive document and has refused to meet with Congressional staff. Instead, Kirkland has devoted its time to compiling a laundry list of legally specious claims of privilege. Notwithstanding Kirkland’s lack of cooperation, we will use every tool at our disposal to pursue this investigation—in this Congress and the next,” wrote the lawmakers. Kirkland has failed to produce any written agreement memorializing its $125 million deal with the Trump Administration beyond President Trump’s Truth Social posts. Absent a written agreement, Trump continues to be the sole arbiter of Kirkland’s legal obligations under the deal. As the lawmakers point out, Kirkland’s professional judgment is necessarily compromised when it is under constant threat of being deemed in violation of its personal agreement with the famously vindictive President. To resist congressional oversight, Kirkland provided vague, contradictory and legally unsound privilege claims that are not supported by legal precedent. The lawmakers reject each of these sham claims in detail. Requests for client identities, hours worked and the value of services do not implicate attorney-client privilege. Kirkland’s attempt to extend executive privilege to dealings with Trump’s personal lawyer, Boris Epshteyn, is unsupported by legal precedent. Kirkland’s claim of a settlement privilege is similarly flawed as they faced no executive order when it entered negotiations, and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) acknowledged in federal court that it engaged in informal information gathering, not an investigation. The lawmakers are renewing their demands for records and answers concerning Kirkland’s negotiations with the Administration, communications with the President’s personal lawyer, Boris Epshteyn, free legal work for federal agencies, potential conflicts with existing clients and efforts to poach attorneys and clients from Paul Weiss while it faced Trump’s retaliatory executive order. They also seek an itemized response to outstanding questions, a detailed log supporting any privilege claims and written confirmation that Kirkland is preserving relevant records, including encrypted or disappearing-message communications. The inquiry continues an investigation Raskin and Blumenthal launched in April 2025 into Trump’s coercion of major law firms and the deals firms struck to avoid retaliation. Joined by Schiff, they subsequently scrutinized firms’ free legal work for the Commerce Department, sought records of Epshteyn’s role in Kirkland’s deal and pressed Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom LLP over potential conflicts involving its work for Intel and the Commerce Department. The full text of the letter can be found here and below. Dear Mr. Ballis: We write for the sixth time regarding Kirkland & Ellis LLP’s (Kirkland) decision to preemptively surrender to President Donald Trump and enter into a legally dubious settlement agreement with the Trump Administration. We have repeatedly requested information and documents about Kirkland’s conduct, including with respect to: (1) Kirkland’s attempts to poach attorneys from a rival law firm that was being extorted by the Trump Administration; (2) Kirkland’s contacts with President Trump’s personal legal fixer, Boris Epshteyn; (3) Kirkland’s commitment to perform $125 million in pro bono legal services that align with President Trump’s political agenda; and, Kirkland’s seemingly unlawful provision of legal services to the U.S. Department of Commerce. To date, Kirkland has not cooperated with our legitimate oversight requests. Your firm has failed to produce a single responsive document and has refused to meet with congressional staff. Instead, Kirkland has devoted its time to compiling a laundry list of legally specious claims of privilege. Notwithstanding Kirkland’s lack of cooperation, we will use every tool at our disposal to pursue this investigation—in this Congress and the next. To comprehensively rein in presidential abuses of power through legislative actions, Congress and the American people must learn the full circumstances and nature of Kirkland’s indefensible submission to an out-of-control executive. Why did Kirkland enter into this agreement? What was promised and by whom? And how did the President’s coercion work in practice? Against that backdrop, we address your counsel’s latest response to our congressional staff, dated May 28, 2026, which raises a multitude of vague, contradictory, and legally unsound objections. I. Attorney-Client Privilege In the May 28 response, Kirkland objects to responding to our requests for records concerning your pro bono engagements and the provision of other free legal services, contending that it would “reveal client confidences, privileged communications, and attorney work product.” Relying on a Third Circuit decision, United States v. Liebman, you argue the privilege extends to our requests because the documents “would convey the substance of attorney-client communications.” As an initial matter, in the context of a congressional investigation, Congress is not obligated to recognize common law privileges, has never formally done so, and no court has ever held to the contrary. But Kirkland’s position is also plainly inaccurate. Although Kirkland fails to specify which of our requests implicate the attorney-client privilege, even a cursory examination of our requests makes it readily apparent that no such privilege is implicated. By way of example, we previously requested a list of pro bono matters that Kirkland has undertaken for the U.S. government, non-governmental clients who have been offered pro bono services pursuant to Kirkland’s agreement with President Trump, and a dollar value of the pro bono services rendered. We similarly requested a list of the federal agencies that Kirkland has performed work for, the number of hours spent working for those agencies, and the billable value of those hours. These requests simply do not implicate any applicable privilege. As Kirkland should know—because it is in the very case that you cited—“It is well established that ‘absent unusual circumstances the identity of the client does not come within the attorney-client privilege.’” As the Liebman case and others demonstrate, the attorney-client privilege does not apply to legal requests—including our requests—that “merely request[] the names of clients who paid fees.” Nor does the attorney-client privilege prohibit disclosures quantifying the “amount of a fee,” or “general information about the nature of the services performed.” Accordingly, please comply with the oversight requests reflected in our prior letters no later than October 29, 2026, including, but not limited to, the following: April 18, 2025, letter: A detailed description of all requests for pro bono services you have received from the White House or any executive branch agency since entering into an agreement with the White House, including the nature of such request, the identity of the individual requesting the services, and the services your firm has agreed to provide. September 24, 2025, letter: A list of the number of hours that Kirkland has contributed to the Commerce Department or the U.S. Government to date. March 2, 2026, letter: A list of all federal agencies that Kirkland has performed work for, the number of hours spent working for those agencies, and the billable value of those hours. II. Executive Privilege In Kirkland’s May 28 response, you contend that Kirkland cannot respond to our requests because they “seek documents related to negotiations conducted on behalf of the President,” arguing, “executive privilege requires an opportunity for the President to assess whether to assert privilege over any of the materials sought and to intervene as necessary.” Once again, that is incorrect. In support of this radical expansion of the executive privilege, Kirkland relies entirely on a statement issued by a minority of D.C. Circuit judges in denying a motion for rehearing en banc. As you well know, that statement has no precedential value and provides no legal basis for withholding documents that Congress has identified as critical to its legislative function. Your response also obscures the more fundamental issue with Kirkland’s assertion—the firm was primarily negotiating with someone outside the Trump Administration. It was dealing with Donald Trump’s personal lawyer, Boris Epshteyn, whom Trump Administration officials have identified as leveraging his proximity to the President to orchestrate multiple “pay-to-play” schemes. No court has held that the presidential communications component of executive privilege extends to communications with private advisors. But Kirkland’s assertion goes even beyond that farfetched claim, arguing that because someone might advise the President, all of Kirkland’s communications with that advisor similarly implicate executive privilege. Kirkland’s theory could functionally exempt any communication by drawing a line, however attenuated, to a President’s advisor—irrationally expanding a narrow privilege. Such a transformation is clearly unworkable, unsupported by any legal precedent, and raised either in error or in bad faith. The same holds for our request for a list of Trump Administration officials that Kirkland communicated with involving these matters. This narrow request did not seek the disclosure of the content of the President’s communications—or for that matter, the disclosure of any government official’s communications—and cannot implicate any executive privilege. To be clear, Kirkland’s communications with government officials would, almost entirely, not be subject to executive privilege. But here, our requests do not even implicate those communications. Accordingly, please comply with the oversight requests reflected in our prior letters no later than October 29, 2026, including, but not limited to, the following: March 2, 2026, letter: All communications from Kirkland, or its agents, with Boris Epshteyn or his agents or associates, including but not limited to, meetings records, phone calls, emails, text messages, or letters. March 2, 2026, letter: A list of all individuals or entities who corresponded with Kirkland, or any of its agents, to discuss an agreement with the Trump Administration, including the date(s) of any and all contacts. III. Settlement Privilege In Kirkland’s May 28 response, you object to the production of communications among Kirkland, the Trump Administration, and Administration representatives that were “made for the purpose of negotiating a mutually acceptable settlement of the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission’s (EEOC) inquiry and anticipated Executive Order.” Kirkland argues that “[a]ny communications made in furtherance of settlement are privileged.” In support of that argument, Kirkland cites a Sixth Circuit case, Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. v. Chiles Power Supply, Inc., for the broad proposition that “confidential settlement communications are a tradition in this country.” To be clear, this is an overbroad, and likely inaccurate, representation of federal law. As other courts have recognized, the Goodyear Tire decision “has not been widely followed.” Indeed, as determined by a D.C. federal court, advocates for a federal settlement privilege have failed to “demonstrate a broad consensus in support of such a privilege.” As you undoubtedly know, the Federal Rules of Evidence governing settlement negotiations are rules of admissibility for federal courts, not privileges. Moreover, congressional investigations are simply not bound by the Federal Rules of Evidence that underlie Goodyear and related cases. Even if we recognized the federal settlement privilege—which we emphatically do not—the unpublished decision you cited in further support of your argument strongly weighs against the application of the privilege here. Specifically, in Baker v. Secretary, U.S. Department of Transportation, the Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit concluded that a district court was permitted to consider communications between an individual and a federal agency in the context of an employment dispute, observing the settlement privilege did not apply because “no formal complaint had been filed.” Similarly, Kirkland was not the subject of a formal complaint at the time it entered into “negotiations” with the Trump Administration. Although you have previously referenced resolving an “investigation” by the EEOC, the EEOC admitted in federal court that the letter it sent to Kirkland and others “constituted informal information gathering and were not a component of any investigation.” Nor was Kirkland subject to an executive order at the time it entered into its agreement or contract with the President. Kirkland has made no effort to explain why a “negotiation” privilege should attach to its conversations with the Trump Administration about the resolution of a voluntary request and a nonexistent executive order. Accordingly, please comply with the oversight requests reflected in our prior letters no later than October 29, 2026, including, but not limited to, the following: April 6, 2025, letter: Did you approach the Trump Administration regarding a preemptive settlement to avoid an executive order against Kirkland, or did they approach you? Please describe in detail the timeline of your engagement with the Trump Administration. April 18, 2025, letter: All records referring or relating to any executive order threatened by President Trump against Kirkland and efforts by Kirkland to negotiate an agreement with President Trump, including but not limited to: Any communications regarding any threatened executive order or any proposed agreement; Any communications with any officials in the Trump Administration from March 1, 2025, to the present regarding any threatened executive order and any proposed agreement; and Draft records constituting or related to any proposed agreement between President Trump and Kirkland. Deliberative Process In Kirkland’s May 28 response, you cursorily argue that Kirkland cannot produce documents related to settlement negotiations because you are not “at liberty to waive any deliberative process privilege that the Administration wishes to assert.” In support of this contention, you summarily cite a district court decision, Matter of Nelson, but neglect to quote from the decision or make even the slightest effort to analogize the facts and reasoning to the present matter. Since Kirkland has failed to explain the case cited in your own communications, we will do so here. The deliberative process privilege is a “limited privilege in several different ways.” First, the privilege “belongs only to the government.” This means that “private parties”—like Kirkland—“can neither assert nor waive the privilege.” Second, it applies “only to that group of communications within the agency or department.” Your communications plainly did not occur within any agency or department of the United States. Third, the privilege must be “lodged by the head of the department which has control over the matter,” a requirement designed to “insure that the privilege remains a narrow privilege which is not indiscriminately invoked.” Your attempt to assert the government’s deliberative privilege process here as a private party is an “indiscriminate” invocation of the privilege. Fourth, there must be a “specification of precise and certain reasons for the need to preserve the confidentiality of the documents at issue.” You have not provided such reasons explaining why communications effecting a shakedown by the President of the United States warrant protection. In sum, this government privilege is completely irrelevant and unavailable to you. Accordingly, please comply with the oversight requests reflected in our prior letters no later than October 29, 2026, including, but not limited to, the following: April 6, 2025, letter: All records referring or relating to President Trump’s March 14, 2025, Executive Order “Addressing Risks from Paul Weiss,” including but not limited to: Any communications regarding the March 14, 2025, Executive Order; and Any communications with any officials in the Trump Administration from March 14, 2025, to the present concerning law firms other than Kirkland. April 18, 2025, letter: Please describe in detail the circumstances surrounding your April 11, 2025, agreement with President Trump. Who facilitated your April 11, 2025, agreement with President Trump? Did Kirkland representatives meet with President Trump or members of his Administration? If so, describe in detail who participated in the meeting(s), when and where they took place, and what was discussed. Did you acknowledge any wrongdoing for representing causes President Trump finds objectionable? Rules of Professional Conduct In Kirkland’s May 28 response, you cite the American Bar Association’s (ABA) Model Rules of Professional Conduct to justify withholding communications requested by the Committees, arguing that Kirkland “take[s] seriously our ethical obligations to our clients and [is] committed to representing them with the highest standards of professional responsibility.” It is fair to question whether Kirkland’s leadership consulted the ABA Rules before it agreed to enter into a personal agreement with the President of the United States to perform $125 million worth of legal services. Indeed, a plethora of ABA Rules would have counseled against entering into such an agreement. For instance, the ABA directs attorneys to act with “courage and foresight” to “shape the body of the law to the ever-changing relationships of society.” The ABA further directs lawyers to exercise their professional judgment “free of compromising influences and loyalties,” emphasizing, “neither the lawyer’s personal interests, the interests of other clients, nor the desires of third persons should be permitted to dilute the lawyer’s loyalty to the client.” Most relevant here, lawyers must be alert to and disregard third parties who seek to exert “strong economic, political, or social pressures upon the lawyers.” Kirkland’s abject failure to reject an unprecedented, extortionate attempt by the President to control the legal profession, an attempt that multiple other law firms successfully rejected and resisted, implicates numerous professional responsibilities of lawyers, and none more so than its duty not to subject the judgment of the firm, and the interests of its clients, to the whims of a highly volatile and vindictive President. Critically, Kirkland has failed to produce any written agreement between the Trump Administration and Kirkland beyond what is contained in the President’s Truth Social posts. That leads us to believe that there is no other written agreement. Assuming that is the case, President Trump appears to be the sole arbiter of what is required by the putative “contract” and what would constitute a violation of the professional rules. Under these circumstances, Kirkland’s professional judgment is necessarily compromised as it must always consider the impetuous desires of President Trump—a third party who wields enormous economic and political pressure over Kirkland—as demonstrated by your decision to succumb to this extortionary agreement in the first place. This is borne out by your representation of the Department of Commerce—a representation that was never announced as being part of the scope of the agreement—as well as press reports that the President has a “broader understanding of the terms” of the contract than what is publicly known, including requiring capitulating firms to represent him in a personal capacity. Kirkland cites a D.C. Bar opinion to further justify its decision to withhold documents from Congress. Again, Kirkland does not appear to have thoroughly vetted the materials it cited. In that very opinion, the D.C. Bar determined an attorney had not violated his ethical obligations by producing documents containing client confidences and secrets to Congress. To be clear, we have not requested materials containing client confidences or secrets, but even if we had, the D.C. Bar’s opinion confirms that the D.C. Rules of Professional Conduct do not prohibit attorneys from complying with congressional oversight requests. The D.C. Bar’s reasoning for reaching its conclusion is instructive. Because Kirkland apparently has failed once again to thoroughly explain the opinion it cites, we offer an explanation of the relevant principles here. In determining that an attorney could disclose client confidences in response to a congressional request, the D.C. Bar relied on Supreme Court precedent holding that “a contempt of Congress cannot be cured by the lawyer’s later compliance with the subpoena,” as well as the Supreme Court’s holding that “when a witness refuses to answer a question in a mistaken, good faith belief that it would violate his rights to be compelled to answer, his mistake of law will be no defense at a trial on the criminal contempt charge.” Kirkland should be mindful of these precedents as it carefully considers its obligations in responding to requests from Congress. Accordingly, please comply with the oversight requests reflected in our prior letters no later than October 29, 2026, including, but not limited to, the following: April 6, 2025, letter: Did members of your firm have contact with known Paul, Weiss clients about securing new or additional business from those clients from March 14, 2025, to March 20, 2025? If so, which members of your firm and which known Paul, Weiss clients? If so, please describe the nature of those conversations, including who initiated them, whether members of your firm made an effort to secure new or additional business in light of the executive order entered against Paul, Weiss, and any subsequent action taken in light of these conversations. If so, please detail the extent to which you or other Kirkland attorneys sought or received any ethical guidance surrounding seeking new or additional business from clients of a firm facing an unconstitutional executive order, including from any state, federal, or other bar association. April 18, 2025, letter: What were the specific terms of the deal Kirkland agreed to with President Trump? Does President Trump’s April 11, 2025, social media statement accurately reflect the terms of your deal? Please detail all client relationships Kirkland has chosen to end from April 11, 2025, to the present. September 24, 2025, letter: Explain whether Kirkland notified clients adverse to the Administration of Kirkland’s work for the U.S. Government.
