Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), the first Senator from California to serve on the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry in three decades , visited Canada this past week for a Congressional Delegation (CODEL) trip to share concerns about the impact that U.S.-Canada trade disruptions are having on California’s industries, including on agricultural goods like wine and dairy products. Senator Schiff sought to learn more about Canada-California collaboration, shared experiences from California farmers and producers he’s met while serving as Senator, and discussed expansion opportunities for California businesses in Canadian markets. “I met with officials to talk about the trade dispute with the United States and the different tariffs, and also to convey the sentiments of my California constituents and how they’re feeling the impacts…[and] to understand the Canadian reaction and how Canadians are feeling about U.S. products as well as the United States of America. I went there not to negotiate USMCA or any trade agreement, but rather to talk about the [Canadian] boycotts on alcohol, and how this is having a particular impact on the wine industry… [and] disputes over dairy, disputes over beef, and other products between our countries, our mutual energy reliance, and other issues. And I found the visit to be incredibly illuminating and helpful,” said Senator Schiff about his trip. Canada is one of California’s largest trading partners and export markets, with cross-border commerce supporting California industries including technology, aerospace, agriculture, manufacturing, transportation equipment, and consumer goods. California and U.S. wine, for example, have generated upwards of $1 billion in annual sales in Canada in recent years. However, California farmers and producers have been disproportionately impacted by bans on the sale of U.S. alcohol by some Canadian provinces. Senator Schiff visited Alberta to meet with the province’s Premier Danielle Smith, Agriculture Minister Tara Sawyer, and Utilities Minister R.J. Sigurdson. Schiff visited a rodeo breakfast in Edmonton and flipped pancakes for attendees alongside Premier Smith. Schiff then traveled to Ottawa, where he met with Canadian Minister for Agriculture Heath MacDonald and Member of Parliament Mona Fortier. Schiff also met with staff at the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa, the American Chamber of Commerce—which promotes American trade and investment in Canada—and American businesses in Canada. Background: Senator Schiff has previously raised concerns about the impact that bans on U.S. alcohol placed by Canadian provinces have had on California agriculture. In June, he wrote to the Premier of Québec saying, in part, “I have had the great fortune of spending time with and learning about the challenges and opportunities of California’s winegrowers. They take great pride in their work, are essential to the state and national economy, and have brought tremendous value – in culture and in taste – to Americans and Canadians alike. Reopening the market to American wine would restore consumer choice and signal a commitment to restoring fair and balanced trade for Québecois consumers and American wineries who have no connection to the underlying trade disputes.” View photos from the trip below: ###

San Francisco, CA — This week, U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) discussed his view on rapidly developing AI capabilities and the role of Congress in regulating the technology during an interview with Punchbowl News co-founders Jake Sherman and Anna Palmer at the publication’s first-ever Tech Summit in San Francisco. In the wide-ranging discussion, Schiffhighlighted his legislation to ensure private industry pays for the energy they use amid the buildout of data centers – so that Americans are not forced to pay higher energy costs as a result of the AI boom – and discussed Democrats’ approach to AI oversight next year, noting that Americans should “expect constructive oversight, not destructive oversight.” Schiff also discussedthe risks he sees in rapidly advancing AI models and argued that concerns about competition with China should include prioritization of safety, developing a skilled workforce, and improving education. View the full interview here . Key Excerpts: On Democrats’ AI priorities should control of Congress flip: […] I think the industry should expect constructive oversight, not destructive oversight. I think it should expect a Democratic majority that wants technology to succeed, wants these jobs to stay in America, wants their contribution to the economy and medicine and science but believes in regulation. Does not believe that any group of people be by dint of their wealth are empowered to make decisions affecting all of society for themselves. I think that’s what they should expect. […] What I do want to see is oversight that leads to sensible regulation of an industry that can do a lot of good and can do a lot of harm. To minimize the harms, to protect against the harms, do what government is supposed to do. I want to see a Congress that does what we have done in the past when we also had massive powerful corporations but we’re not afraid to regulate them. That is a basic function of government. On why Congress must move quickly to put guardrails on advanced AI: […] I do think we need to put in place protocols and monitors, a system to make sure that as these frontier models are developing, they’re developing safely. That there are processes in place where we don’t have to simply take the word of the companies that ‘don’t worry we’re doing it safely.’ I certainly don’t believe the self-policing; the moral authority argument is sufficient. There’s just too much profit motive, too much of a collective action problem that confronts the whole industry globally. […] You train the power of AI to find out everything it can about a single individual. Do we really think that their health records or their purchases or their subscriptions or any of their data is beyond the reach of an AI agent, sophisticated model, trying to find out the personal information? And with all the Flock cameras and with all the other CCTV cameras and the vulnerability of those systems, are we going to have any privacy left? And I think unless Congress acts, there won’t be any privacy left. On ensuring AI development is safe as we compete with China to establish AI dominance: […] I get that we should be very concerned about China’s advances in this area. I don’t want to dismiss that argument. That’s an argument that says that we need to reach some kind of an accord with China, which won’t be easy to do, but we need to do our best. It is not an argument though that, because China is making advances and we want to stay ahead of China, that we should rush headlong with the development of these models and regenerative AI in such a way that well, ‘let’s be sure that if we kill ourselves we do it first rather than letting China do it.’ We still want to make sure what we’re doing is safe for our people and safe for others. […] Why don’t we focus on improving our education system? Improving STEM education, making sure that everyone who graduates from high school has a good solid education, that the doors of higher education are open. Let’s compete with China on a skilled workforce. Let’s compete with China in how we think about the integration and the manufacturing of products that will incorporate AI. That’s where a lot of the economic benefits are going to come. On passing legislation to protect Americans from absorbing higher costs from data center buildouts: […] I introduced an early bill on this that would insist essentially that these data centers pay their own way. That they not only develop their own energy, but also that they have additional capacity to put energy into the grid during peak times. That they are responsible for the upgrades to the regional system that those costs are not socialized to others. It’s not hard to require that. It’s certainly not going to be done just by some kind of, ‘well, we give you our word.’ […] There should be complete transparency. I don’t think people should be misled about a project and then suddenly learn it’s going to be a data center in their backyard. But I don’t think everywhere is the same and I think communities should make the decision. Do they want it? Do they not want it? And some communities may want it, and many will not want it and that ought to be a decision that is made locally and I think not nationally. But we should be insistent nationally that those costs and burdens not be socialized onto others. On the Senate’s latest proposal for permitting reform: […] We absolutely need permitting reform, and it looks like we may be close. What I’m going to be particularly looking at, and the text was just released, so we’re all kind of digging through it, is this going to be just regulatory reform for the oil and gas industry? Is this really just going to be used to advance those two sources of energy or, is this going to be advantageous to renewables? And what about in an administration in which there is almost a theocratic objection to anything but oil and gas? We’ve seen our state punished repeatedly by this president who only represents those states that he won. Is that going to continue? Are there any meaningful limits on that in this permitting reform? That’s what I’m going to be looking at. ###

Washington, D.C. — U.S. Senators Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Gary Peters (D-Mich.), along with U.S. Representatives Gus Bilirakis (R-Fla.-12) and Frank Pallone (D-N.J.-06), led over 100 lawmakers in sending a bipartisan, bicameral letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio urging the State Department to prioritize the release of Armenian detainees being unlawfully held in Azerbaijan. “We are concerned that amid these positive steps Azerbaijan continues to undermine the peace process. Azerbaijan’s decision to sentence the unlawfully detained Armenian prisoners of war demonstrates a willingness to upend stability. Additionally, the presence of Azerbaijani military forces in more than 200 square kilometers of Armenian territory creates asymmetry in ongoing talks,” the lawmakers wrote. Those being detained include political and military leaders of Nagorno-Karabakh who have been illegally imprisoned since Azerbaijan’s attack on the region in 2023. Additionally, the letter calls on Secretary Rubio to advocate for the removal of Azerbaijani military forces from within Armenia. Currently, Azerbaijan maintains a military presence in over 200 square kilometers of land within Armenia. Furthermore, the letter instructs the State Department to withhold military assistance from Azerbaijan if the government remains uncooperative on addressing these issues. “The United States has a critical role in ensuring that ongoing talks yield results that advance peace and security in the region,” the lawmakers continued. “As Azerbaijan continues to unlawfully detain Armenian hostages, destroy Artsakh’s ancient Christian heritage, and occupy Armenia’s sovereign territory, the U.S. should not be subsidizing the very regime responsible for these abuses. Instead, Washington should use its leverage to hold Baku accountable for its aggression and advance a truly just, durable, and dignified peace in the South Caucasus,” said Aram Hamparian, Executive Director of Armenian National Committee of America. “The ANCA thanks Senator Peters, Senator Schiff, and Representatives Bilirakis and Pallone for leading this bipartisan, bicameral call to withhold U.S. military assistance to Azerbaijan. The support of 101 Members of Congress on this letter sends a clear message: Azerbaijan’s destabilizing conduct and repeated violations of international law must not be rewarded with U.S. taxpayer dollars.” “The extent of bipartisan and bicameral support reflects a clear recognition in Congress that U.S. policy toward Azerbaijan must be grounded in accountability and measurable outcomes. The unlawful detention of Armenian hostages remains a serious humanitarian and rule-of-law concern that has direct bearing on U.S. policy. Section 907 equips the government with leverage that should ensure U.S. military assistance to Azerbaijan is aligned with concrete progress toward accountability, regional stability, and a durable peace. Congress has sent a clear signal that these concerns warrant sustained attention by the Administration’s engagement in the region. U.S. policy should guarantee a lasting peace,” said Mariam Khaloyan, Director of Congressional Relations at the Armenian Assembly of America. Background: Tuesday, June 23, 2026 marked 1,000 days since Armenian prisoners of war and civilian hostages were unlawfully detained by Azerbaijan following the ethnic cleansing of Artsakh (Nagorno-Karabakh) in 2023. At least 19 Armenians are still held as POWs and 120,000 civilians were forcefully displaced. California is home to nearly 250,000 Armenians – more than half of the Armenian diaspora in the United States – and Senator Schiff has been a strong champion for the Armenian community, leading Congress to formally recognize the Armenian Genocide in 2019. Schiff has consistently submitted provisions to be included in the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) to bring home Armenian POWs following Azerbaijan’s ethnic cleansing of Artsakh in 2023. He will continue pushing for the release of POWs. Most recently, Schiff urged the Department of State to highlight Azerbaijan’s human rights abuses in its Country Reports on Human Rights Practices for 2025 and push for an end to Azerbaijan’s continued human rights violations. The full text of the letter can be found here and below. Dear Secretary Rubio, We recognize the work this administration has done to mediate peace negotiations between Armenia and Azerbaijan. Furthermore, we note efforts by Armenia and Azerbaijan to resolve longstanding border disputes through consistent talks. However, we are concerned that amid these positive steps Azerbaijan continues to undermine the peace process. Azerbaijan’s decision to sentence unlawfully detained Armenian prisoners of war demonstrates a willingness to upend stability. Additionally, the presence of Azerbaijani military forces in more than 200 square kilometers of Armenian territory creates asymmetry in ongoing talks. This context illustrates Azerbaijan’s fragile commitment to the process and emphasizes the importance of the United States remaining engaged on this issue. As Azerbaijan’s conduct threatens to compromise the integrity of the peace process, we note with concern the recent decision to reauthorize the waiver of Section 907 of the FREEDOM Support Act [U.S. Public Law No: 102-511]. Despite the issuance of the waiver, we urge your administration to withhold U.S. military assistance to Azerbaijan if they continue to jeopardize the success of negotiations. The United States has a critical role in ensuring that ongoing talks yield results that advance peace and security in the region. In February 2026, Azerbaijan sentenced 16 Armenian detainees to extended terms ranging from 15 years to life in prison. These sentences followed a series of trials that were widely rebuked by international human rights organizations, legal experts, and the European Parliament as a miscarriage of justice. Azerbaijan continues to imprison scores of domestic journalists, opposition leaders, and activists on politically motivated and unfounded charges. The decision to proceed with the trials and sentencing of Armenian detainees is consistent with Azerbaijan’s practice of denying fundamental due process and rule of law. The detainees included political and military leaders of Nagorno-Karabakh who have been held illegally since Azerbaijan’s military assault on the region in 2023. Almost three years have passed since Azerbaijan’s attack on Nagorno-Karabakh forcibly displaced over 100,000 Armenian inhabitants in what has been widely characterized as an act of ethnic cleansing. In addition to forced displacement there continue to be reports of the destruction of Armenian Churches in Nagorno-Karabakh. The pattern of cultural erasure in the region and the decision to move forward with sentencing these individuals calls into question Azerbaijan’s genuine commitment to long term peace and stability. On April 29, 2026, Armenia and Azerbaijan held the thirteenth meeting to discuss border delimitation. Addressing longstanding border disputes remains a critical task to ensure the stability of any future peace agreement. So far, the only practical outcome from these talks has come from Armenia’s efforts to address Soviet-era territorial disputes. In May of 2024 Armenia returned four Azerbaijani enclave villages that had been under Armenian control since the first Karabakh war. However, these efforts have been complicated by Azerbaijan’s ongoing occupation of an estimated 241.4 sq kilometers of Armenian territory, following military encroachments into Armenia in 2021 and 2022. Azerbaijan’s recent encroachments and entrenched military presence within Armenia’s internationally recognized borders presents a security challenge and sets the stage for asymmetric negotiations. A just outcome to these talks is imperative to maintaining the integrity of Armenian sovereignty and ensuring long-term stability in the region. We encourage the administration to use existing leverage, such as withholding military assistance, to ensure positive outcomes. Following a White House summit with the leaders of Armenia and Azerbaijan last year, the waiver of Section 907 of the FREEDOM Support Act was extended. Although the summit was an important step in the right direction there is still significant work to be done to address unresolved humanitarian and security issues. It is clear, that the decision to waive Section 907 has not induced Azerbaijan’s engagement on ensuring the release of detainees. As a result, we are concerned that Azerbaijan’s inconsistent behavior jeopardizes the prospect of a just and long-lasting peace in the region – and that the continued waiver of Section 907 without a commitment to addressing these concerns will only further encourage destabilizing actions. June 23rd, 2026, marked the 1000th day of unlawful detention for the Armenian prisoners in Azerbaijan’s custody. It is imperative that the United States applies meaningful pressure on Azerbaijan to ensure their release, as required under international law. We call on the administration to engage with Azerbaijan to secure the release of detainees and encourage the removal of Azerbaijani military forces from sovereign Armenian land. If meaningful steps are not taken, we urge your administration to withhold U.S. military assistance in order to demonstrate the United States’ commitment to ensuring all parties take the peace process seriously. We thank you for your consideration and look forward to the opportunity to work with you on efforts to ensure peace and stability in the region. ###

Schiff on the need for bipartisan action on AI regulation: “Increasingly, as people hear from their constituents, there’ll be bipartisan interest in legislating this area.” Washington, D.C. – This week, U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) detailed his AI priorities during an appearance on The Verge’s Decoder Podcast with Nilay Patel. During the interview, Schiff highlighted the need for enforceable industry-wide guardrails that protect against the potential harms of frontier AI development and underscored that voluntary commitments like the framework put forward by Donald Trump would not be enough. Schiff also noted that if control of Congress changes, Democrats will pursue oversight of harmful AI incidents, noting: “You’re going to see vigorous oversight in this area… We’re going to want the leaders of this industry to come in and talk about all of the times that their own agents have gotten away from them, how it happened, what’s been done about it, and what they’re doing about it. We’re going to want these companies to be transparent with Congress about it.” The Senator also voiced support for the establishment of a regulatory body designed with the high expertise and discretion necessary to keep up with advanced model development. View the full interview here . Key Excerpts: On how Congress’s failure to regulate social media should inform its approach to putting guardrails on AI: I’ll be honest, very circumspect about Congress and legislating the tech sector because we did such a — I don’t know what language I’m allowed to use here — but such a shitty job when it comes to any kind of regulation of the harms, the societal harms coming out of social media. We’re going to have to do a much better job and much more quickly when it comes to AI, because the threats are even more significant and we’re already at the point of strong potential harms. It can’t wait. We certainly can’t take the kind of years we’ve taken to try to even wrap ourselves around social media. On how Democrats would conduct tech industry oversight if control of Congress flips: You’re going to see vigorous oversight in this area to begin with. We’re going to want the leaders of this industry to come in and talk about all of the times that their own agents have gotten away from them, how it happened, what’s been done about it, and what they’re doing about it. We’re going to want these companies to be transparent with Congress about it. We’re going to want to legislate in this area, and that may come into conflict with the president, but there’s a lot of bipartisan work product here. And I think that given where the country is and where it’s moving, it becomes increasingly difficult for this president to veto bipartisan work product coming out of the Congress. So that is my hope. It’s certainly a far better prospect than we have today. This is going to be a very central priority for the American people. We want to harness AI for the good it can do. We want to use it to bring down the cost of things. That’s our central priority. And there are ways that AI might be useful in bringing down certain costs. We want to protect the dignity of work also, but we want to make sure that this doesn’t pose a threat to the American people. On Trump’s voluntary AI regulatory framework not being enough to match the threat of frontier advancements: It was interesting to see all those tech leaders there signing onto this voluntary pledge on the one hand and on the other hand, away from the White House grounds, away from the president, being very public and saying, “We need regulation. We don’t want this to be just ‘Trust us, we’ll do the right thing.’” So yeah, it was very distant, very jarring. None of these companies want to incur the wrath of this very vengeful president. Apparently, they will say what he wants them to say in his presence. But the reality is, there is a real national security threat here. As these models become more and more advanced, as they advance themselves through this recursive AI, we have less and less of a sense of what they’re doing, how they’re deciding what they’re deciding, and what they’re trying to access lawfully or unlawfully. That is a national security concern of the highest order. There are other security concerns too. On the need for a regulatory body to keep up with advanced model development: This debate is going to keep evolving as AI evolves and at a speed that is really much faster than Congress has proven capable of legislating. I like to say that in the technology world, Moore’s law is increasing productivity, doubling it every 18 months, and with AI, maybe that’s quadrupling it every five months. The legislative calendar works more on a Murphy’s law timetable. And I think that disparity is even more pronounced in the area of AI. What I think that translates into is that we’re going to need a regulatory body that has real discretion and real expertise that can move a lot quicker than Congress can. Whether that looks like an FDA for artificial intelligence or some other agency, I think that’s ultimately going to be necessary. That agency’s going to have to have real power and teeth and real expertise. It’s going to be a challenge, as with these independent monitors: if there’s a government component there, how do we afford that? Because there’s so much talent, and that talent can draw much bigger salaries in the private sector. But I do think we’re going to need a regulatory body in addition to whatever the overarching statutory framework is. On the need for enforceable industry-wide regulation of AI and data center build outs: Data centers are the most tangible way for people to express their concerns about their neighborhood, but also about their job, about the technology, and about the uncertainty of it all. And I think the initial concern, and I still think it’s quite a dominant concern, is over the impact on jobs and the nature of work. But what has reached the fore more recently is concern about runaway AI and the danger it poses. What will the concern look like a month or two months from now? I don’t know, but I do think it’s not going away. And as the AI bills — and I’ve introduced several — indicate, not just mine, but others, most of those bills are bipartisan. […] My bill on the data centers would force them to pay the costs so that consumers don’t have to. It’s not the voluntary, “we pledge, we might, we’d like to; just don’t provide anything that will force us to observe those costs.” Those are mostly democratic bills. Republicans have largely adhered to the president’s line about not posing any real imposition. They want to pass fig-leaf kind of stuff, but not real stuff. But I think increasingly, as people hear from their constituents, there’ll be bipartisan interest in legislating this area. ###

Washington, D.C . – U.S. Senators Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) introduced a resolution to designate October 2026 as Substance Use & Misuse Prevention Month in America. The Senate passed the bipartisan resolution on September 30. “Substance use and misuse affect millions of Americans each year, from every community and of all ages,” said Senator Schiff. “I am proud to join Senator Ricketts in supporting crucial prevention programs to combat the drug addiction and overdose epidemic in our country.” “Substance abuse is a public health issue with terrible consequences for Nebraskans,” said Senator Ricketts. “Our loved ones and communities suffer from illegal drug use. Just last year, substance abuse affected nearly 45 million Americans. We can and must do more. This bipartisan resolution raises awareness of abuse and the need to support prevention efforts.” The full text of the resolution can be found here . ###

Schiff: “This war must end. Not just for the sake of the higher costs this war has imposed on the American people, but for the sake of those servicemembers who have paid an even higher price. Those who have been asked to miss holidays, birthdays, births and weddings for nearly a year in order to sustain this war of choice.” San Diego, CA — Today, U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) issued the following statement on the return to port of the USS Abraham Lincoln , which was deployed to the Middle East for more than 300 days during the ongoing Iran War: “321 days. That’s how long the USS Abraham Lincoln and its thousands of servicemembers have been away from their families and their home port of San Diego. And today, for the first time in 10 months, they return home. They hug loved ones. They sleep out of harm’s way. “In the time these men and women were deployed as the tip of the spear in the Iran War, they worked tirelessly. And that service took a heavy toll – a price we have come to know through harrowing stories shared by family members and even the military’s own leadership. The crew of the Abraham Lincoln has faced long and grueling shifts, diminished supplies and even mental health crises. Those burdens of such a long deployment have been shouldered by the crew and their families back in San Diego. “As we welcome them home today, and we hear more of those stories of hardship and sacrifice, I hope these heavy burdens resonate through the halls of the White House and the Pentagon. With no clear objective and no measurable progress, this war must end. Not just for the sake of the higher costs this war has imposed on the American people, but for the sake of those servicemembers who have paid an even higher price. Those who have been asked to miss holidays, birthdays, births and weddings for nearly a year in order to sustain this war of choice. “Only last week, the USS Theodore Roosevelt and its carrier strike group left San Diego. All signs point to its crew being relief for a beleaguered force still deployed in the Middle East. I hope for the sake of our sailors, Marines, soldiers and airmen that this new deployment of Californians does not repeat the hardships of the Abraham Lincoln.” Background: Senator Adam Schiff has pushed the Department of Defense on the Abraham Lincoln ’s prolonged time away from its home port of San Diego. In August , he joined Senator Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) and U.S. Representatives Scott Peters (D-Calif.-50), Juan Vargas (D-Calif.-52), Mike Levin (D-Calif.-49), and Sara Jacobs (D-Calif.-51) in a letter to the Department of Defense Office of Inspector General seeking more information regarding Carrier Strike Group 3’s deployment. Schiff also recently highlighted constituent stories from servicemembers’ families on the Senate Floor, emphasizing how the prolonged deployment of the USS Abraham Lincoln has sent shockwaves throughout the San Diego community as he continued his call for an end to the Iran War. ###

Washington, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senators Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla (both D-Calif.) and U.S. Representative Salud Carbajal (D-Calif.-24) are seeking answers from former White House energy adviser Brittany Kelm who, after spending months advancing the interests of Sable Offshore Corporation’s (Sable) unlawful California project in her capacity at the White House, has now taken a top job as Vice President of Policy and Commercial Programs at Sable. “To understand whether your transition directly from the White House and Department of Interior to Sable – including your work on Administration policies before you left office and at Sable on matters related to your role on the NEDC after your separation – complies with the federal ethics laws, we seek detailed information regarding your interactions with the company during your government service, as well as documents and communications about your recent hiring by and employment with the company,” the lawmakers wrote. While at the White House, Kelm publicly championed and supported efforts to advance the restart of Sable’s pipeline in California, a project that has not been permitted under California law, has incurred fines, and had court orders against it. Sable CEO Jim Flores thanked Kelm for her work helping to restart the company’s oil production, a move the lawmakers argue is a violation of state law. “These public statements leave the distinct impression that you were closely working on the Sable deal at a time when you could leverage the work you did advancing Sable’s business interests to secure private employment or other financial benefits from the very company you supported as a government official. To move from a high-level government office to its direct beneficiary, especially for the purpose of personal gain, is both ethically improper and potentially unlawful,” the lawmakers continued. The lawmakers emphasize that “federal law prohibits any government employees from participating in any particular government matter, including permitting decisions, contracts, and other matters involving the interests of named parties, in which a company with whom they are seeking or negotiating for future employment has a financial interest.” The lawmakers demand Kelm preserve all records of communications between her and Sable and question whether she received any ethics or conflicts of interest guidance. Senator Schiff has been a strong opponent of restarting oil drilling off the California coast and has repeatedly pressed Sable for answers on the company’s collaboration with the Trump administration to invoke the Defense Production Act (DPA) in relation to this project. The full text of the letter can be found here and below. Dear Ms. Kelm, We write to you in your personal capacity to seek information related to your recent move from the White House’s National Energy Dominance Council (NEDC) to the oil industry as Vice President of Policy and Commercial Programs at Sable Offshore Corporation (Sable), where you will reportedly oversee their Washington, D.C., policy office. Your new role, considering your prior close relationship with Sable while serving as a White House Senior Policy Adviser for Oil and Gas, raises serious questions about your compliance with federal ethics laws, compounding the many existing legal issues with the federal government’s unilateral grant of approval of pipeline rights to Sable. To understand whether your transition directly from the White House and Department of Interior to Sable – including your work on Administration policies before you left office and at Sable on matters related to your role on the NEDC after your separation – complies with the federal ethics laws, we seek detailed information regarding your interactions with the company during your government service, as well as documents and communications about your recent hiring by and employment with the company. During your tenure at NEDC, you and others made several statements suggesting that you were instrumental to the White House’s efforts to advance Sable’s pipeline in California by utilizing the Defense Production Act to override California’s objections to the pipeline. For instance, at a June 2026 press conference, Sable Chief Executive Officer Jim Flores reportedly thanked you personally for helping restart the company’s oil production, and you thanked Sable for “trusting the Trump Administration.” According to your own LinkedIn posts, you also visited Sable’s operations on at least two occasions and, while still in your role as a government official, you even appeared in photographs wearing Sable-branded merchandise. After Department of Energy Secretary Chris Wright signed a secretarial order directing Sable to open its Santa Ynez Unit pipeline, you posted online “[w]e are bringing more US production online ASAP us 🛢️ let’s go Sable Offshore Corp.” When announcing your departure from the White House, only days before beginning work at Sable, you referred to yourself as a “deal closer,” while a White House colleague praised you for “never [giving] up on Sable Offshore Corp.” These public statements leave the distinct impression that you were closely working on the Sable deal at a time when you could leverage the work you did advancing Sable’s business interests to secure private employment or other financial benefits from the very company you supported as a government official. To move from a high-level government office to its direct beneficiary, especially for the purpose of personal gain, is both ethically improper and potentially unlawful. As you must know, federal ethics laws and regulations restrict certain conduct by current and former executive branch employees. In particular, federal law prohibits any government employees from participating in any particular government matter, including permitting decisions, contracts, and other matters involving the interests of named parties, in which a company with whom they are seeking or negotiating for future employment has a financial interest. After an employee leaves government, they are permanently restricted from communicating to or appearing before the federal government on behalf of any other person concerning any particular matters involving specific parties in which a former employee participated “personally and substantially” while serving in government. Additionally, ethics laws impose a two-year restriction on representing private entities regarding specific matters that were pending under an employee’s “official responsibility” during their final year of federal service, as well as establish “cooling off” periods that prohibit senior officials from contacting high-ranking White House personnel to influence official actions, regardless of whether they worked on those matters previously. Against this legal backdrop, your public involvement in matters affecting Sable and rapid transition from the White House to Sable raise serious questions regarding your compliance with federal ethics requirements governing impartiality, employment negotiations, recusals, and post-government employment. Sable’s conduct in recruiting and hiring you also may bear on the legality of their efforts to secure federal government approval of a dangerous oil pipeline project whose operation has run afoul of state laws and court orders. We therefore request that you preserve all records and communications relating to Sable or any of their officers, employees, or agents, from March 1, 2025, to the present and continue preserving such materials on an ongoing basis. This preservation hold applies to all relevant records within your possession related to all communications with Sable, any person representing or purporting to be acting on behalf of Sable, or any consulting firms associated with Sable. This includes, but is not limited to, records and communications via email, whether official or personal; mobile devices; encrypted or disappearing messaging applications; social media; calendar entries; meeting notes; and voicemail and text messages. To the extent that you use any autodelete functions, you should immediately suspend auto-delete functions and notify persons with control over potentially relevant records of similar preservation obligations. Given your reported involvement with Sable during your tenure at NDEC, please provide written responses to the following questions, including requested documents and communications, by October 21, 2026: What role did you play in efforts to restart Sable’s project during your time in government, and what actions did you take to assist Sable? Please provide detail about your role, titles, and a complete timeline of communications between yourself, Sable, or any person affiliated with Sable. What matters relating to Sable fell within your responsibility as NEDC’s Senior Policy Adviser for Oil and Gas? Did anyone at the White House, NEDC, or any federal agency discuss with you your obligations under applicable ethics laws, regulations, and policies at any point in your tenure? If so, identify each person involved and please describe what was communicated and when did those communications begin? When did you first communicate with Sable or its representatives regarding potential employment? Please detail those communications and provide all related records. Did you file a financial disclosure report, including a public report (OGE 278e) or confidential disclosure report (OGE 450)? If so, please provide the last copy of the report that you filed with any agency of the United States including the Executive Office of the President or the Department of the Interior. Pursuant to Section 17 of the STOCK Act regarding negotiations for post-government, non-federal employment, did you file notice with any federal entity concerning your employment negotiations or agreement with Sable? If so, please provide a copy. Did you disclose to the Department of Interior, Office of Government Ethics, the Executive Office of the President, or any other federal entity your employment agreement or arrangement with Sable, including the date on which it was reached? If so, please provide a copy, including the date of the disclosures, and any advice you received. Did you receive ethics guidance concerning Sable, including any guidance concerning seeking or negotiating for future employment, any guidance concerning social media or endorsement of companies, or any post-employment guidance? If so, please provide a copy of any written guidance, a full summary of any oral or verbal guidance, and identify all persons with knowledge of the exchange. Did you recuse yourself from any matters involving Sable during your time at NEDC? If so, please describe the matters, when you recused, and provide all records related to your recusal including any recusal statement or ethics advice. While seeking employment with Sable, did you seek or obtain a waiver or other authorization under 18 U.S.C. § 208 or 5 CFR § 2635.605? What steps are you taking to comply with the post-employment restrictions proscribed in 18 U.S.C. § 207? To your knowledge, did the White House, NEDC, Department of the Interior, Office of Government Ethics or any other federal entity provide you or Sable with guidance identifying the matters on which you are prohibited from working after government service? If so, please provide a copy of any written guidance, a full summary of any oral or verbal guidance, and identify all persons with knowledge of the exchange. Have you sought or received any additional ethics or conflict of interest guidance since departing federal service? If so, please provide a copy of any written guidance, a full summary of any oral or verbal guidance, and identify all persons with knowledge of the exchange. The White House stated that you do not plan to work on any “ongoing official matters” between Sable and the administration in your new role at Sable. Yet, your new job title according to LinkedIn is Vice President – Policy & Commercial. What will you be working on in your new role at Sable, if not federal policy matters? Have you communicated in any way with the federal government in this new role or have you advised others on communications with the federal government? Thank you for your prompt attention to this matter. As Members of Congress, we take seriously our constitutional duty to investigate and root out potential waste, fraud, and abuse across the executive branch. Your thorough and prompt responses to these inquiries are critical to these efforts, as they may inform our work on legislative solutions to strengthen federal government ethics standards, enhance transparency, and reform applicable conflict-of-interest statutes. We look forward to your response, including a written confirmation that you are preserving all records related to this congressional inquiry . ###

Washington, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) issued the following statement on the third anniversary of the October 7 attack by Hamas on Israel: “Three years ago, Israel was the victim of a terrorist attack by Hamas that killed nearly 1,200 civilians. Innocent lives were snuffed out, families murdered in cold blood, women raped, young people targeted because of who they are and where they called home. “But the violence of that day did not end on October 8. Its violence was contagious, plunging the region into chaos and years of war that have taken a toll on many thousands of people — Palestinians and Israelis. Israeli civilians were held hostage in dark tunnels by Hamas for hundreds of days, while being subject to rape, torture and murder. Palestinian civilians lost their lives as whole neighborhoods were destroyed, and they continue to endure, unimaginable conditions in Gaza; Palestinians still suffer increased violence and displacement in the West Bank. Civilians in Israel still live in fear of another promised attack by Hamas terrorists, and civilians in Northern Israel or Lebanon worry about being collateral damage in the continuing struggle between Israel and Hezbollah. “After three years, the pathway to peace and a lasting two-state solution is farther out of reach and tattered, while extremist voices have flourished in the Middle East. “This anniversary should be a solemn moment to recommit to the goal of two sovereign states, and rebuilding the pathway to that future. Just as we pushed to bring hostages home and achieve a ceasefire, we must continue to push for expanded aid to rebuild Gaza, for an end to Hamas’ ability to threaten Israel, and for a lasting agreement to end this conflict and ensure that Israelis and Palestinians may live side by side in peace, security, dignity, and mutual recognition.” ###

Glendale, CA – Today, U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) joined congressional colleagues and entertainment unions at Glendale’s historic Alex Theatre to rally for the passage of the bipartisan, bicameral, Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act , legislation to create a federal film tax incentive. “I am here to tell you that we have never been this close to getting a federal tax credit passed – never been this close. I’ve been working on this in Congress for almost 25 years…We have never had such broad bipartisan support, and look, this support is just across the board. We have the support of the President, we have the support of the White House, we have the support of Spencer Pratt and Jon Voight. We have the support of labor unions across the spectrum, and in the U.S. Senate, I’m proud to tell you that as of this moment, there are 12 U.S. senators who are co-sponsors of this legislation,” said Senator Schiff during his remarks. “A study published just this week found that the share of production spending by U.S. studios on movies that are made primarily or partially in the U.S. declined from 74 percent to 24 percent over the last quarter century. That is a staggering loss in the industry, but this tax credit, which is a base credit of 20 percent, with additional 5 percent credits going up to 30 percent of a tax credit, is layered upon whatever the state of California or other states do. That is powerful enough for the first time to really bring not just TV production back, but film production back, and all of the multiplier impacts that has on the economy. So we know our mission. We’ve got to get this done,” Senator Schiff continued. Background: For years, Schiff has highlighted the need to increase film production in America and has continued to build bipartisan support in Congress for his federal film incentive proposal. On September 24, 2026, Senator Schiff introduced the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act alongside Senator Tim Scott (R-S.C.) to create a federal film tax incentive to keep film and television production in the United States. During his time in the California State Senate, Schiff helped lead efforts to increase film production in California and protect local jobs. As a member of the U.S. House of Representatives, Schiff spearheaded efforts in Congress to extend California’s film tax credit, including in 2014 when he led 28 members of the California Democratic delegation in urging the leaders of the California State Senate and Assembly to reauthorize and enhance the tax credit. In 2024, Schiff sent a letter to the Bureau of Economic Analysis and the Bureau of Labor Statistics requesting detailed data on the impact of foreign production incentives on the domestic industry. In March 2026, Senator Adam Schiff hosted a spotlight hearing in Burbank, California to highlight the importance of bolstering American film production and tackling the challenges including generous tax incentives provided by other countries. Bakersfield, CA — U.S. Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), published an op-ed in The Bakersfield Californian condemning the Trump administration’s policies and rhetoric that have fueled the uptick in targeted hate and violence against Sikh Americans. In his op-ed, Schiff points to the recent escalating and alarming actions across the nation, including the recent stabbing of a Sikh truck driver from Sacramento at a Wyoming rest area, the recent openly discriminatory social media posts by the Department of Homeland Security, and the tightening of requirements for non-domiciled Commercial Driver’s Licenses — a targeted attempt to deprive members of the Sikh community of their livelihoods. “The most powerful tool in our arsenal to combat this hatred is one we can all use — our voices. Speaking up forced the administration to remove some of the racist posts that fuel the kind of violence we witnessed in Wyoming. Let’s keep speaking out. I stand with the Sikh community. And I ask you to join me,” Senator Schiff wrote. Background: Earlier this year, Schiff traveled to Bakersfield specifically to meet with Sikh truck drivers, businesses, and community members to talk about the ongoing threat of losing their commercial driver’s license (CDLs) and the impact this has on their livelihoods, community, and local economies. Schiff expands more on this in his op-ed. Read the full op-ed here and below: The Bakersfield Californian : SEN. ADAM SCHIFF: The Sikh community and the tragic consequences of a policy born of bigotry By U.S. Senator Adam Schiff California is fortunate to have a thriving community of Sikh Americans who have helped our state flourish: building businesses, shaping California’s booming agriculture industry, holding leadership positions in civil service, and so much more. But while their contributions are woven into the fabric of America, this community has also confronted dangerous hate in the place they call home. One terrible tragedy, driven by such hate, just took place. Just days ago, a Sikh truck driver from Sacramento was stabbed repeatedly in the bathroom of a Wyoming rest area. This violence came just four days after President Trump’s Department of Homeland Security shared a now-deleted social media post that painted the entire Sikh community as a threat — telling them to “self-deport or find out.” The post was abhorrent, and the link to real violence against the Sikh community is hard to dispute. In a country founded on the ideal that “all men are created equal,” the Trump White House and DHS have turned starkly away from our Founders’ vision. They have implemented policies that deny Sikh Americans opportunities to earn an honest living and applied pressure and provocative rhetoric to deliberately target and hurt this community. And now, more than half a million Sikh Americans are scared — looking over their shoulders on the street or afraid to show up for work because of the dangerous environment that these policies and practices have created. The Trump administration has pushed an agenda that is openly xenophobic. The DHS website urged citizens to report undocumented drivers, while displaying an image of a Sikh man, as if people could look into the cab of a truck and identify whether someone was a citizen or not. The plain implication was that if someone was Sikh, they should be presumed to be violating the law and be reported. In addition to these hateful practices, the administration has used other punitive measures to discriminate against the Sikh community. In January 2025, DHS rescinded restrictions limiting immigration enforcement at “protected areas.” This change exposed Sikh gurdwaras, and other houses of worship, to Immigration and Customs Enforcement surveillance and arrests — potentially chilling religious expression and practice. The administration then decided to tighten requirements for non-domiciled Commercial Driver’s Licenses — a targeted attempt to deprive members of the Sikh community of their livelihoods. And when California did not capitulate to the federal government’s unreasonable demand to cancel thousands of CDLs — many of which impact Sikh drivers — the administration threatened to withhold $160 million in federal funds. Yet, the U.S. Department of Transportation’s own data shows that these drivers have a better safety record than most other drivers. None of this is about safety. In a meeting with Sikh truck drivers in Bakersfield, Sikh leaders told me that community members have been hit hard by the administration’s policy and political attacks on their community. “We’re actually more afraid now and subject to more abuse now than we were after 9/11,” a community member confided in me. In the aftermath of that deadly attack on America, the Sikh community — which played no role in the attacks — experienced terrible hatred and discrimination. Twenty-five years later, the community feels even more under siege as a result of the rhetoric directed against it by leaders in the highest positions of our government. This is un-American and unacceptable. In our nation’s 250 years, we have battled this kind of hostility and prejudice before. We have taken on institutional policies that reinforced it. And in this moment, we must look to that history as we confront a new variation on an old hatred. We must stand up for our neighbors — the Sikh workers, students and families who are at risk from this rhetoric and these harmful policies. The most powerful tool in our arsenal to combat this hatred is one we can all use — our voices. Speaking up forced the administration to remove some of the racist posts that fuel the kind of violence we witnessed in Wyoming. Let’s keep speaking out. On behalf of the Sikh community, the Latino community, the Haitian community, and every other community in America that has become the target of choice for dehumanization by this administration. I stand with the Sikh community. And I ask you to join me. ###

Washington, D.C. — U.S. Senators Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla (both D-Calif.), joined U.S. Senators Michael Bennet (D-Colo.), John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.), and Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) and U.S. Representative Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.) to introduce the Stop Orphaned Wells Act, legislation that would prevent oil and gas companies from abandoning oil wells on public lands, a practice that shifts well cleanup costs from oil and gas companies to the American taxpayer. “Oil companies can’t just walk away from abandoned oil and gas wells and leave taxpayers to bear the cleanup costs,” said Schiff. “I’m joining Senator Bennet and other colleagues to make sure that Big Oil is responsible for cleaning up their messes. Americans should not have to deal with the consequences of an oil company’s negligence.” “Across California, there are over 5,000 orphaned oil wells that pose a threat to the health and safety of our communities and the environment,” said Padilla. “When wells are left abandoned, drinking water is polluted, greenhouse gases are emitted, and the climate crisis is accelerated. This bill will help ensure orphaned oil and gas wells are plugged so Californians and communities across the country are protected from toxic emissions and contaminated air and water.” “For too long, taxpayers have footed the bill to clean up abandoned wells after companies walk away from their responsibilities,” said Bennet. “As the Trump administration moves to weaken the safeguards that hold companies accountable, Congress must protect taxpayers and the public lands that power Colorado’s outdoor economy, while making sure oil and gas companies pay the cost of cleanup, rather than Colorado’s future generations.” “Trump asked oil and gas executives to bankroll his campaign with a $1 billion contribution in exchange for a big payback. Meanwhile, Americans are left footing the bill for the damage they leave behind,” said Ansari. “Orphaned wells threaten our water, wildlife, and air. I’m proud to lead the effort alongside Senator Bennet to make the oil and gas industry clean up its own mess. Our bill would ensure oil and gas companies pay to clean up the wells they abandon.” “Abandoned wells put Colorado communities in danger,” said Hickenlooper. “As Governor, we capped as many of these wells as we could, and that work continues here in the Senate, where we’re protecting taxpayers from getting stuck with the bill. Capping wells creates jobs and lowers pollution. It’s a win-win.” “In New Mexico and across the country, abandoned wells pose serious environmental harm and threaten the health of our communities,” said Luján. “We must ensure that oil and gas companies are held accountable and that taxpayers are not on the hook for the cost of cleanup. I’ve long fought to address abandoned wells, including championing the REGROW Act that was passed into law, and continue to work to ensure we identify and plug the thousands of abandoned wells nationwide. That’s why I’m cosponsoring this legislation to prevent companies from abandoning their wells and help reduce the number of abandoned wells in New Mexico and across the country.” “When an oil and gas company goes bankrupt, New Mexicans shouldn’t be the ones left to pick up the tab for cleanup costs,” said Heinrich. “Right now, the Trump administration is making it easier for these companies to walk away without enough money set aside to clean up their wells. The Stop Orphaned Wells Act ensures that companies set aside money to meet their cleanup responsibilities, so taxpayers aren’t left paying the bill.” Until 2024 when the Biden administration added agency rules, oil and gas fiscal assurance requirements were minimal, leading companies to abandon wells instead of remediating the land after drilling. The Trump administration is now rolling back these essential protections for public lands and American taxpayers. Nationwide, there are currently over 140,000 documented orphaned wells, including more than 15,000 on federal lands, and hundreds of thousands more that may be orphaned. Additionally, the number of documented orphaned wells in the United States has more than doubled since 2020 . These sites are not only a significant liability for taxpayers and a growing threat to water resources, air quality , wildlife habitat, and private lands, but also jeopardize public health, ecosystems, grazing lands, outdoor recreation sites, and cultural resources that are at high risk from contamination. In Colorado alone, there are nearly 1,400 orphaned wells, with almost a third of these wells on federal or Tribal lands. Estimates from Colorado’s Energy & Carbon Management Commission predict that it could cost over $36 million to clean up all of the existing orphaned wells on federal and Tribal lands in Colorado. Moreover, there are currently 245 idled federal wells in Colorado that have the potential to eventually become orphaned, which could cost taxpayers approximately $23 million to remediate. Due to new leasing policies enacted by Congress in 2025, executive orders to increase federal oil and gas drilling, and the financial assurance rollback, industry is likely to drill as many as 3.8 million wells on national public lands in the coming years, and to then pass as much as $753 billion in potential financial liabilities back onto local communities and taxpayers. The Stop Orphaned Wells Act builds on Bennet’s Oil and Gas Bonding Reform and Orphaned Well Remediation Act and recent state-level reforms in Colorado , New Mexico, Texas , and Utah to fix this broken system and close long-standing industry loopholes around orphaned wells. This legislation would ensure operators, not taxpayers, pay for cleanups and aligns directly with the interests of Western voters, nearly 9 in 10 of whom believe oil and gas companies should cover reclamation costs once drilling ends. “In La Plata County, orphaned wells are a nuisance for property owners and a danger for people and animals alike. This bill builds on Colorado’s innovative work to ensure that federal regulation protects our communities, livestock, and wildlife – and prevents this public health issue from happening in the first place,” said Marsha Porter-Norton, La Plata County Commissioner. “The Board of County Commissioners strongly supports Senator Bennet’s Stop Orphaned Wells Act. When a well is abandoned, local communities must shoulder the risks to their health, environment, and taxpayer dollars. This legislation provides the accountability needed to ensure oil and gas companies, not our community, pay to restore the lands they use,” said Jody Shadduck-McNally, Larimer County Commissioner and Chair of the Board of County Commissioners . “Adams County is glad to see Senator Bennet leading the charge on this significant bipartisan issue, as it is of critical importance to our communities. Our county has the second highest number of orphaned wells in the state; taking action to preserve the health and safety of both our residents and our environment is a top priority for our Board. We look forward to working with the Senator in honing this legislation to be as helpful and effective as possible,” said Commissioner Julie Duran Mullica, Chair of the Adams County Board of Commissioners. “Like countless places across the country, San Miguel County has been forced to clean up after reckless operators. Orphaned wells are not only an unfair burden on our taxpayers but also a dangerous polluter of our beloved natural resources and public lands. Senator Bennet’s bill takes long-overdue actions to strengthen regulations and hold irresponsible companies accountable,” said Galena Gleason, San Miguel County Commissioner. “The Stop Orphaned Wells Act is urgently needed in Western Colorado, where orphaned, non-producing wells irresponsibly emit harmful methane gas and harm our health, air and water quality, and critical wildlife habitat. This Act will finally make producers responsible for properly closing, remediating, and reclaiming lands after they stop producing oil and gas,” said Lynn Padgett, Ouray County Commissioner. This legislation is supported by 20 organizations, including Earthjustice Action, Colorado Fiscal Institute, Conservatives for Responsible Stewardship, Conservation Colorado, Montana Wildlife Federation, National Parks Conservation Association, Natural Resources Defense Council, Nevada Wildlife Federation, New Mexico Wildlife Federation, Public Land Solutions, Rocky Mountain Wild, San Juan Citizen’s Alliance, Sierra Club, Taxpayers for Common Sense, Trout Unlimited, Western Colorado Alliance, Western Organization of Resource Councils, Western Resilience Center, Wild Montana, Wilderness Workshop, and The Wilderness Society. In addition, this legislation was endorsed by U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee. The text of the bill is available HERE . A summary of the bill is available HERE . Additional stakeholder quotes are available HERE . ###
